articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admits to having an affair with suspected Chinese spy
articles.content: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with a woman who is allegedly a Chinese spy in a letter to Nvidia staff, which we have below. Nvidia released a statement from the company's board of directors late on Sunday to address the report that U.S. intelligence believes Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy . While Nvidia has no reason to believe that sensitive corporate information or U.S. national security was compromised, the company intends to examine all available information to determine what happened. The BoD claims that it is fully confident in Jensen Huang and his leadership team. Huang fully supports the investigation. "A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation," a statement by Nvidia's BoD reads. "The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders. […] Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it." A report earlier on Sunday claimed that the U.S. intelligence agencies believe that Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who was allegedly recruited by China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) to gather information and help Chinese companies obtain restricted AI accelerators. Megaspeed has been on the radar for smuggling restricted hardware for China since at least 2025. Nvidia has rejected suggestions of improper dealings, said that its CEO regularly meets thousands of customers and that these interactions do not involve sensitive corporate information or national security secrets. Chinese officials have also dismissed the espionage allegations as unfounded. Neither the alleged romantic relationship nor the suspected intelligence operation has been independently recognized as a fact. "I owe my family and all of you an apology," Huang wrote in his X post. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry. Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it. To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust." In June 2018, Intel chief executive Brian Krzanich resigned after an internal investigation, assisted by external legal counsel, confirmed that he had engaged in a consensual romantic relationship with an Intel employee, which violated the company's non-fraternization policy applicable to all managers. Krzanich, who had led Intel since 2013, also stepped down from the company's board, while then-chief financial officer Robert Swan took over as interim CEO. Jensen's letter to staff reads as follows: To my colleagues at NVIDIA, I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry. Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it. To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust. To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that…
articles.author: Anton Shilov

articles.title: Lenovo and HP run out of RTX 5090 gaming desktops as standalone GPUs disappear from US retailers
articles.content: Lenovo and HP show no readily purchasable RTX 5090 desktop configurations Amazon advertises an available ASUS RTX 5090 graphics card for $7,679.80 Several retailers list RTX 5090 cards at more than twice launch prices Nvidia's GeForce RTX 5090 is becoming increasingly difficult to purchase across the United States, with Lenovo and HP facing availability problems affecting their premium desktop computers. A quick check of both manufacturers' US online stores found no readily purchasable desktop configurations equipped with Nvidia's flagship consumer graphics processor. The situation extends beyond manufacturer websites, as several major retailers are also displaying expensive standalone RTX 5090 graphics cards as unavailable. Lenovo and HP struggle with RTX 5090 availability HP's OMEN MAX 45L illustrates the high cost of obtaining a complete computer equipped with the graphics processor through manufacturer-operated stores. The company lists its RTX 5090 configuration at $7,999.99, offering an AMD Ryzen 9 processor , 64GB memory, and 4TB of combined storage. Despite its premium specifications, HP's US website identifies the desktop as out of stock, preventing customers from purchasing the advertised configuration. Lenovo's US online store also showed no readily purchasable RTX 5090-equipped desktops during the availability investigation. The difficulties extend to standalone graphics cards, which offer consumers an alternative to purchasing expensive complete computers from established manufacturers. The growing scarcity of Nvidia's RTX 5090 is driving substantial price increases, with graphics cards originally launched at $1,999 now appearing at several retailers for considerably higher amounts. Newegg lists several RTX 5090 graphics cards sold directly by the retailer as unavailable, including MSI's Suprim model and ASUS's TUF Gaming edition. Although neither card is currently available directly from the retailer, their listed prices stand at $5,899.99 and $5,099.99, representing increases of approximately 195% and 155%, respectively. B&H Photo Video reports similar availability problems, with its ASUS TUF and MSI Gaming Trio OC RTX 5090 models temporarily out of stock. The retailer lists the two graphics cards at $4,599.99 and $4,499.99, respectively, representing increases of approximately 130% and 125% over Nvidia's original launch price. Amazon currently has the ASUS TUF Gaming RTX 5090 available for purchase at $7,679.80, approximately 284% above Nvidia's original launch price. TUF Gaming GeForce RTX 5090 Graphics Card: $7679.80 As RTX 5090 scarcity pushes prices higher, this ASUS TUF model costs $7,679.80, offering 32GB GDDR7, PCIe 5.0, HDMI 2.1b, DisplayPort 2.1b, and Axial-tech cooling. View Deal Independent manufacturers still offer expensive alternatives However, the availability problems affecting Lenovo and HP do not mean US consumers can no longer purchase complete computers containing RTX 5090 graphics cards. Best Buy continues advertising several configurations from independent computer manufacturers, including Skytech and CLX, with available purchasing options. One Skytech Tempest desktop combines an AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D processor, 32GB memory and the RTX 5090 for $8,999.99. Another Skytech Blaze 5 configuration costs $9,379.99, while a CLX SET desktop featuring an AMD Ryzen 9 9900X3D carries a $9,849.99 price. Newegg also advertises Skytech computers containing the graphics processor, including configurations priced between $9,299.99 and $9,699.99. Dell similarly maintains RTX 5090 availability through its Alienware Area-51 desktop range, although some configurations exceed $10,000. One version featuring Intel's Core Ultra 9 285K processor, 32GB memory and 2TB of storage costs $10,499.99. Another configuration featuring an AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 processor, 64GB memory and 4TB of storage carries a $13,499.99 price. articles.title: Lillith Tells Your Future
articles.content: Maybe you are old enough to remember Zoltar in an arcade, or perhaps you’re just a fan of the movie Big. Either way, maybe you’d like to build an animated fortune teller. [Oh Well Why Not] did just that and gives you a roadmap for you to make your own. It took four months to build, but with the road already mapped, you can probably do it in less. Then again, who can predict the future? The fortune teller, Lillith, uses servos and some voice generation to provide the same experience. If you dare to hit the button, you’ll get a glimpse into your future that’s at least as good as a fortune cookie from your local takeaway place. Lillith doesn’t hide behind windows since it isn’t in a public venue, but if you were going to put it out in the wild, you’d probably want to encase it a little better. While waiting, the servos provide some small animations to attract the next user. If you remember Bullwinkle more fondly than Zoltan, you might prefer this project .

articles.title: Parents Sue Google Over AI Safety Risks On School Chromebooks
articles.content: The New York Times reports: After chatting for months with Google's artificial intelligence on a school-issued Chromebook laptop, a 13-year-old student made plans to end her life, according to a lawsuit filed in California Superior Court on Monday, the latest in a wave of litigation over Big Tech's effects on young people. The lawsuit, which refers to the girl as Emma, said that her parents first learned she had access to Google's AI in mid-March after their daughter's school sent a message warning them that she was in "imminent danger" of self-harm. Emma's mother logged into the teen's school Google account and found her daughter composing a suicide note on Google Docs, the complaint said. Her parents, named as John and Jane Doe in the lawsuit, immediately took Emma for an emergency psychiatric evaluation, and she now goes to therapy every week. Emma, a seventh grader in Charlotte, North Carolina, had grown convinced that she had multiple mental health disorders following interactions with AI Mode, a chatbotlike feature on Google Search, the complaint said. She also searched for "what is a suicide note" and made comments like "I am planning my own funeral" to the AI, the complaint said. The lawsuit is likely the first to claim that Google "hastily integrated" AI features into company apps used on K-12 Chromebooks, Google-powered laptops provided to millions of children by U.S. school districts, while failing to notify their parents of the potential risks... The case underscores how public school districts have come to depend on classroom laptops, tablets and apps from companies like Google and Microsoft for teaching and learning. In recent years, some Big Tech companies have used their own infrastructure in schools to promote their AI chatbots for teachers and students. The new lawsuit argues that Google's "sprawling digital ecosystem" of laptops and apps has enabled the tech giant to spread its Gemini AI chatbot across public schools — as well as turn on some students' access to AI features by default — without parents' awareness or permission. While school administrators can toggle company apps like YouTube and Gemini on or off for students in different grades, school administrators have complained that Google's system has not allowed them to disable AI Mode and AI Overview, features that are embedded in Google Search... The new lawsuit against Google is part of a wave of litigation this year over Big Tech's effect on young users... Several parents have also sued AI companies over allegations that their children died by suicide following interactions with chatbots. In a possibly-related development, Google announced a new policy of disabling its AI tools by default for schools this week. And schools that re-enable searches will have a new choice, the New York Times points out: "to enable student access to the AI features that the company has already embedded in search or to a new AI feature intended to assist students with schoolwork." But Google still isn't offering schools an option to turn off AI altogether in search, a company executive told the New York Times, because "search and AI are deeply integrated." Thanks to long-time Slashdot reader theodp for sharing the article. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: This is the cheapest RTX 5090 PC we could find — and why we'd pick it over a similarly-powered laptop
articles.content: The complete desktop costs $70 less than Amazon's listed ASUS graphics card CyberPowerPC bundles a desktop RTX 5090 with 32GB DDR5 memory Mobile RTX 5090 laptops sacrifice performance compared with desktop graphics cards Nvidia's GeForce RTX 5090 has become ridiculously expensive , with standalone graphics cards selling for several times their original launch prices. That makes finding a complete desktop computer equipped with the flagship graphics processor for less than $8,000 particularly interesting. One configuration currently available from CyberPowerPC costs $7,609.50 after applying a $400.50 promotional discount. TUF Gaming GeForce RTX 5090 Graphics Card: $7679.80 As RTX 5090 scarcity pushes prices higher, this ASUS TUF model costs $7,679.80, offering 32GB GDDR7, PCIe 5.0, HDMI 2.1b, DisplayPort 2.1b, and Axial-tech cooling. View Deal A complete RTX 5090 desktop PC The GeForce Extreme Creator Gaming PC comes equipped with ASUS's TUF Gaming GeForce RTX 5090, featuring 32GB of GDDR7 memory. Interestingly, the ASUS TUF Gaming GeForce RTX 5090 is listed on Amazon for $7,679.80; buyers are basically getting the PC at no cost. The system uses Intel's Core Ultra 5 250KF processor, featuring six performance cores and twelve efficiency cores, alongside a maximum turbo frequency of 5.3GHz. Although this is not Intel's most expensive desktop processor, its specifications provide a capable foundation for demanding gaming and computing workloads. The graphics card receives power from a 1,300W fully modular supply, while an Asetek 570LC liquid cooler handles processor temperatures. The device also includes 32GB of DDR5 memory operating at 6,000MHz, providing sufficient capacity for many demanding applications and modern games. Storage comes from a 500GB Kingston NVMe solid-state drive using PCIe Gen4 connectivity, although buyers might eventually want additional capacity. The remaining configuration includes an ASRock Z890-C D5 motherboard, Wi-Fi 7 connectivity, Windows 11 Home and a CyberPowerPC Onyxia II enclosure. There is also a two-year parts warranty, alongside complimentary service coverage that includes labour and lifetime technical assistance. Importantly, the advertised $7,609.50 price excludes a monitor, keyboard and mouse, meaning buyers should account for additional peripheral expenses. (Image credit: Future) RTX 5090 laptops are cheaper, but there is an important difference One reason this desktop configuration deserves attention is the substantial difference between desktop and laptop versions of Nvidia's flagship graphics processor. Although gaming laptops advertised with RTX 5090 graphics can cost considerably less, their mobile graphics processors are not equivalent to desktop versions. Laptop manufacturers must accommodate restricted cooling capacity, battery consumption and physical dimensions, requiring substantially different power configurations. Consequently, a mobile RTX 5090 generally delivers considerably less graphics performance than its desktop counterpart, despite sharing the same product designation. The desktop RTX 5090 also provides 32GB of GDDR7 memory, giving it considerable advantages for demanding graphics workloads and local artificial intelligence applications. This distinction matters because comparing prices without considering the underlying hardware can create misleading impressions about what buyers actually receive. At $7,609.50, the CyberPowerPC configuration is certainly expensive, although its inclusion of Nvidia's flagship desktop graphics card changes the calculation. With standalone RTX 5090 cards commanding extraordinary prices, this is practically a case of buying the graphics card and getting the rest of the computer free.

articles.title: What to watch Sunday: All the new shows and movies just added to Netflix, Prime Video, HBO Max, and more (Nov. 8)
articles.content: When it comes to deciding what to watch, it can get overwhelming sifting through the best streaming services . So I've compiled a TV guide on what to watch tonight. I've gone through everything from Netflix , Prime Video , MGM+ etc. to see what's recently landed. I've even added some live sports you can stream on some of the best streaming services, along with new shows and episodes premiering today. Here are all the new shows and movies (and live events) you can stream tonight (November 8), and where to watch them. For more picks, check out the five best new to Netflix movies and shows to stream this week . Top picks to stream tonight 'Love is Blind' Season 11 Reunion (Netflix) The latest season of Netflix hit "Love Is Blind" is behind us, leaving another fresh crop of couples (and countless viewers) reeling. While six Bostonian couples got engaged in the "Love Is Blind" season 11 pods, viewers had a hard time rooting for any of them. Instead of getting swept up in the romance, audiences were left spotting one red flag after another as the engagements took an explosive turn. Now it's time to find out what actually happened after the cameras stopped rolling. Hosted by Nick and Vanessa Lachey, the reunion brings the pod squad back together to rehash the past and share updates on their loves lives. The streaming event will also include a live chat, interactive games, and never-before-seen bonus footage from the season. Watch "Love is Blind" Season 11 Reunion on Netflix at 9 p.m. ET 'The Institute' Season 2 Premiere (MGM+) The first season of Stephen King adaptation "The Institute" was a huge hit for MGM+, recording one of the best premieres in the streamer’s history. With the first season having covered the entirety of Stephen King’s original novel, season 2 takes some bold steps beyond the original story, adopting a grander sense of scale with bigger action sequences and a score of new characters to flesh out its twisted sci-fi world. "The Institute" season 2 picks up after Luke Ellis (Joe Freeman) and his fellow escapees break free from Dennison with their sights set on bringing down the Institute once and for all. But the organization is already plotting a comeback, this time with the backing of powerful tech billionaire Nolan Reeves (Alfie Allen). Meanwhile, Ms. Sigsby (Mary-Louise Parker) has been pushed to the sidelines and is desperate to claw her way back into the Institute's inner circle. With fresh threats, buried secrets and new players entering the picture, the battle against the Institute is only getting started. Watch "The Institute" Season 2 Premiere on MGM+ at 9 p.m. ET 'Heart Eyes' (Hulu) Halloween may be over, but if you're still itching for more spooky season vibes, I can't recommend "Heart Eyes" enough. The premise is hokey but fun: Each year on Valentine's Day, a masked serial killer known as Heart Eyes hunts down lovers enjoying the holiday, leaving a trail of brutal murders across the country. But this time, he messes with the wrong couple. For starters, they're not even together. Not yet, anyway, though it won't be long given all the meet-cute romcom movie magic propelling them into each other's orbit. Ally (Olivia Holt), an ad designer recovering from a recent breakup, is forced to work with her hopeless romantic colleague Jay (Mason Gooding) on a big project. But when Heart Eyes mistakenly targets them as the next victims, they find themselves caught up in a deadly game of cat and mouse. The biggest jumpscare came at the end, though, when I saw Josh Ruben, a name any Dropout or College Humor fan will recognize, was in the director's chair. His love of romcoms and horror comes through loud and clear. articles.title: Apple saves $2.7B in taxes by funnelling finances through Singapore
articles.content: Apple has saved $2.7 billion in taxes in 2026 thanks to funneling its finances through Singapore, better than its usual move involving Ireland. Apple Marina Bay Sands, Singapore As a massive multinational, Apple knows a thing or two about taxation and how to minimize its exposure to it. However, while Ireland has been seen as one of its main destinations to cut how much tax it pays, it did even better by using a different territory. In an annual Apple disclosure in line with U.S. reporting rules , the Financial Times says Apple took advantage of the tax incentives in Singapore to a great effect. It funneled about $50 billion in profits through the Asian hub in 2026 alone. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums

articles.title: Salon, One of the Web's Pioneering News Outlets, Shuts Down After 31 Years
articles.content: "It has been an extraordinary privilege," says the subheading on Thursday's announcement. After 31 years Salon.com will stop publishing, according to an announcement which appeared on the site under the byline "Salon". It remembers that Salon "was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier." When Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing. Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own... Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it... To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon's legacy belongs to all of you... The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable... Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today. Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege. Slashdot reader oumuamua remembers Salon as one of the internet's first digital-native publications. Slashdot linked to Salon many times over the years — for example, this 1998 story headlined "Linus Story in Salon". Peter Neves was the first of many who wrote in to tell us about an article in Salon Magazine that describes an "...analogy between MS and the Catholic Church, and Linus and Martin Luther. " The Associated Press remembers Salon as "an early staple of internet discourse." And while Salon told them there were no immediate plans to take down Salon's online archives, the Associated Press notes the site's announcement "did not immediately indicate what would become of its employees, though some reported they had lost their jobs." (Longtime staff writer Amanda Marcotte wrote on her Patreon that she and "everyone" are "the latest victim of AI's predations.") "A spokesperson for the outlet said 19 full-time employees had been affected, as well as a handful of private contractors," writes the Associated Press. Variety adds that Salon "joins later-arriving sites such as Buzzfeed and Gawker that found it difficult to monetize cultural and topical reporting for a general audience and eventually shut down." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: New report claims 'America hates data centers' as it finds 90% of public comments at local government meetings are negative
articles.content: More than 90% of public comments oppose new American data centers Water consumption remains the biggest concern among data center opponents Rural and urban communities oppose data centers for different reasons Public resistance to data center construction is spreading across the United States, with local government meetings recording overwhelming opposition to proposed developments. A new database containing more than 10,000 public submissions indicates that communities remain largely unconvinced about hosting these facilities. Residents' objections focus on the effects of data center construction, particularly water consumption, electricity costs and environmental pollution. Local opposition cuts across political and geographical divisions The American Sentiment website, operated by San Francisco AI startup Prophecy Gov, examined 10,202 public comments collected during 906 meetings across 417 local governments. Its findings cover 48 states with 90.5% of submissions opposing data center developments and only 7% expressing support. Another 2.5% of the comments consisted of questions about the proposed developments, while 73% of meetings recorded no expressions of support from residents. Even where favourable opinions emerged, opponents outnumbered supporters by approximately six to one. The resistance crosses political affiliations, with Republican and Democratic counties recording almost identical levels of opposition. However, disagreements over specific concerns varied according to community characteristics, with rural residents frequently discussing farmland and property rights. Urban and suburban participants more commonly raised concerns involving pollution, electricity expenses, government accountability and inadequate disclosure. Water consumption attracted the greatest attention among opponents, particularly following reports of substantial withdrawals by individual computing developments. One project reportedly consumed 29 million gallons in May 2026, prompting nearby residents to notice reduced pressure across their local water supplies. Microsoft subsequently claimed that its newer artificial intelligence facilities consume approximately the same annual water volume as restaurants. Nevertheless, these competing claims have not eliminated public concerns about resource consumption and the potential consequences for surrounding communities. Technology companies and industry leaders face growing scrutiny Public criticism has also extended to major technology companies associated with artificial intelligence and large computing infrastructure projects. Google, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft featured among the companies mentioned during discussions about proposed developments. SpaceX and xAI chief executive Elon Musk received the most personal references, followed by OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel ranked third, ahead of Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos. Despite the attention given to artificial intelligence, only 21% of submissions mentioned AI, meaning most objections concerned other aspects. Concerns about electricity costs, environmental pollution, water availability and local development therefore featured prominently throughout the collected discussions. Support also varied considerably among occupational groups, with union workers expressing substantially greater acceptance of new facilities. Approximately 79% of commenters identifying as union workers supported data centre construction, compared with just 3% of property owners and residents. Even among people employed directly in the data centre industry, only 40% supported the construction of additional facilities, with these figures indicating employment opportunities have not necessarily translated into widespread public acceptance of new data centre projects.

articles.title: Trevor Noah on AI
articles.content: Trevor Noah, Rana el Kaliouby and Oren Etzioni discuss AI onstage at Boston’s Museum of Science on Oct. 19. (Nicolaus Czarnecki Photography for the Museum of Science, Boston) On Oct. 19, Trevor Noah launched Luminaries , a science conversation series at Boston’s Museum of Science. I joined him onstage, and Rana el Kaliouby moderated. Rana is a pioneer of emotion AI, software that reads human emotion, and the host of the Pioneers of AI podcast . She wrote afterward that she expected Trevor to be witty and funny, but “didn’t expect to be so blown away by his humanity and depth of ideas.” Here are a few of his insights with his own words highlighted. AI often appears deep but merely works on the surface When an AI matchmaker Rana built in ChatGPT picked Trevor as her match, he pointed out that it knew very little about either of them. It assembled a plausible answer from what’s on the internet. “AI is particularly good at seeming like it has gone beneath the surface, when in fact it’s calculating everything above the surface.” Trevor added that when you tell AI it made a mistake, it thanks you but often fails to correct the error: “It’s like a friend who’s been to a lot of therapy but doesn’t actually change.” In-person community is a defense against a dystopian AI future When asked how we protect ourselves from AI’s downsides, Trevor said the answer “goes back to something that is very un-technological and very un-AI.” He cited Robert Putnam’s book Bowling Alone , noting that places where communities form accrue many surprising benefits including more accountable governments. I pushed back that communitarianism , the 1990s movement my father helped found to foster communities, had failed. Trevor responded that we hand too many ideas to intellectuals, who then “apply too much academia” to them. Communitarianism failed, he deadpanned, “because it’s called communitarianism.” An overly academic name. He noted that nobody calls a phone a failure when the first version doesn’t sell; companies keep re-releasing it. He vowed never to stop investing in community. “I don’t need to see if you’re a deepfake, because I’m sitting here with you.” Trevor is optimistic about technology Despite his concerns, Trevor has “yet to see a technology that blew up and then left everyone behind.” Cars, computers and the internet all spread to ordinary people. AI has reached what he calls “work intelligence”: it can do the jobs we invented, but we keep inventing new ones. Salt and ice used to be precious. Now restaurants hand them out for free. What we value changes, and in Trevor’s view, we’re expendable only if we define being human by the tasks we value today. “If we are the people who draw pictures of ourselves on a cave wall, and we sing songs for no reason really, then we’re infinitely capable as creatures.” Our conversation turned to AI’s impact on jobs. The real jobs question is the following distance Touring as a comic, Trevor saw towns hollowed out after Kodak and the automaker Studebaker left. Factory workers were told automation was progress. “White-collar workers are now experiencing what many blue-collar workers experienced for decades,” he said. The difference, he argued, is that white-collar workers are closer to power, so newspapers are covering it. Trevor is confident new jobs will come, as they did after telephone exchange operators disappeared. What worries him is the gap. His analogy is the highway, where the following distance is the space that lets you stop before you hit the car ahead: “There is no job that will last forever. There is nothing that won’t be displaced. The question is, how long is the following distance between the two things?” Trevor tells tech leaders that “it’s easier to be patient when you are in a position of privilege,” and added, “But ironically, they don’t have patience when it comes to quarterly earnings.” Why AI isn’t coming for Trevor’s job After ChatGPT took off, show hosts kept telling him weak…

articles.title: Do Data Centers Have a Smaller Effect on Electricity Prices Than We Think?
articles.content: "According to a new study by researchers at Harvard University and the University of Pennsylvania, data centers are probably having only a small effect on residential electricity prices," reports the Washington Post. "The researchers calculated that these operations were responsible for just 4% of the utility rate increases over the last five years..." There are certainly some areas — like in Pennsylvania, Virginia, Ohio and other states covered by grid operator PJM — where data centers have skyrocketed demand, pushing some costs onto residential customers. But multiple studies by different researchers and organizations have failed to find a strong connection between data centers and the overall trajectory of U.S. electricity prices in recent years. Another analysis earlier this year by researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology found that, between 2010 and 2024, data centers increased average electricity prices for residential customers by just 2.1%. Last year, research from the Brattle Group and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found that data centers were actually decreasing costs in certain regions. And another study by the Electric Power Research Institute found that a doubling of data center capacity between 2019 and 2024 resulted in a 4 percent drop in home electricity prices... The new Harvard and Penn study found a slightly higher impact on industrial electricity prices — the price paid by manufacturers and large facilities. For those customers, data centers were responsible for 15% of the price increase between 2020 and 2025. But for ordinary Americans... the changes simply were not substantial [according to Wharton School professor Serguei Netessine, one of the study's authors]. "So far we have no evidence that data centers increase prices all that much," Netessine said. Instead, he said, prices are rising due to more quotidian factors: rising gas prices, an aging electricity grid, and wildfires and hurricanes requiring improvements to the grid and recovery after disaster... If the number of data centers continue to boom, experts say, residential prices could be affected more down the line. Data center electricity demand is expected to increase steeply over the next few years, requiring new power generation — wind, solar or natural gas — to be put onto the grid. And residents have issues with data centers that go beyond the price of electricity. The new developments have been singled out for loud noise, polluting power generation, and for disturbing residential neighborhoods and natural landscapes. According to the Pew Research Center, more than half of Americans say that data centers are mostly bad for the environment. Others feel that the AI race — which could ultimately leave many Americans out of work — is being forced upon them. "I think generally what we're seeing is a broader range of reasons the public has opposed data centers," [said Ryan Hledik, principal at the Brattle Group]. "Concern about AI leading to loss of jobs — all of that is getting packaged together." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Siri AI Rumored to Become 'More Like an Agent' as Early as Next Year
articles.content: Siri AI is much more intelligent and personalized compared to classic Siri, but it is still not nearly as advanced as proactive, always-on agents like OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse. That may change, though, according to a new rumor. In his Power On newsletter today , Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman said he was told that Apple could make Siri function "more like an agent" as early as next year. However, if this plan moves forward, the exact implementation remains to be seen. "Dots, Muse and Grok can keep track of goals, determine what needs to happen next and continue pursuing objectives without the user initiating every individual step," said Gurman. "Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I'm told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year." Apple's AI ambitions could go beyond making Siri more agentic. In a closed-door meeting in recent weeks, Gurman said that Apple CEO John Ternus told Apple's software engineering chief Craig Federighi that Apple needs to "accelerate" its software roadmap and "move quickly beyond merely making necessary improvements to Siri." articles.title: Google and Microsoft among those signing up to OpenAI's plan for a new website crawling standard — including opting-out of internet scraping
articles.content: Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic say they will honor one robots.txt group as a cross-company opt-out from AI training It governs how content is used rather than whether bots can crawl it, defaults to allowing training, and does nothing for content already scraped Anthropic has started implementing it, OpenAI promises to do so in the coming months, Microsoft starts February 1, 2027, and Google targets 2027, while Meta is supportive but uncommitted Google and Microsoft have joined OpenAI and Anthropic in promising to honor a single line in robots.txt that tells AI developers whether a website's content can be used to train their models. Until now, a site that wanted to say no had to write a rule for each company's crawler, and sometimes for several crawlers run by the same company. The shared signal is meant to replace that sprawl with a single entry that every participating provider reads the same way. That is genuine progress for overworked webmasters, but the promise is narrower than much of the coverage suggests: The new line states a preference about how content may be used rather than stopping bots from fetching it; it is not an approved standard, does nothing about content already collected, and none of the four major players fully honor it yet. Doing the bare minimum with differing definitions of what the commitment entails OpenAI's announcement drew much of the attention, but the company casts itself as one participant among several in an Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) effort, and the mechanism isn't its own. It comes from an Internet-Draft published the same day by Kevin Kelley of Anthropic, which names a policy token, "__usage_ai-training", in the User-Agent line of an otherwise ordinary robots.txt group. Training is defined by the IETF's AI Preferences (AIPREF) working group as the process of changing a generative model's learned parameters, excluding models used purely for tasks such as classification or ranking. OpenAI describes what it will honor as "foundational generative AI training," which sounds narrower than the draft's definition. Calling it a standard may be premature: The IETF's own tracker labels the document an individual draft that the IETF has not endorsed, and that has no formal standing, and it lapses on May 3, 2027 unless revised. Anthropic is the only one of the four major AI players to say it has started. OpenAI aims to implement the signal over the next few months but has given no date. Microsoft will begin honoring the shared preference as it crawls from February 1, 2027, while Google is aiming for 2027. Each company is also wiring the line into its own controls differently. Google says that when a site uses the shared token to opt out without separately specifying Google-Extended, it plans to treat that "as if the publisher had disallowed Google-Extended." Because Google-Extended also governs grounding in Gemini Apps, a site that only wants to stop training could lose its citations and clicks in Gemini answers too, and Search Engine Journal notes that Google's documentation describes no way to separate the two. Interestingly, Microsoft goes the other way. It adopts the shared line for training but adds a separate, page-level AI Grounding preference, including a DisallowExtended option that keeps content available to its own products such as Copilot while excluding the grounding services it sells to other businesses. Meta, not one of the four, has been warmer than it has been about its commitment. Its VP of communications, Andy Stone, called the common signal "an important step," but SiliconANGLE reports the company has not committed to honoring it. The timing is awkward: Meta has pushed back to November 20 revised commercial terms that would let it crawl websites linked to its business accounts, after a backlash forced it to strip training from the listed uses. With training removed but not expressly banned, Sam Quigley of the News/Media Alliance told the Mercury News last…

articles.title: Marketers Are BURNED OUT -  And No One Gives AF
articles.content: I have read countless posts about bloated marketing roles where six jobs are crammed into one title. One listing asked for a “Marketing Manager” to handle brand strategy, paid media, SEO, email marketing, copywriting, and front-end web design. All of that... on a junior salary! These are not rare. They are the norm these days. Scroll LinkedIn or Reddit for five minutes and you will see post after post of people venting about being stretched thin, underpaid, and told to be “grateful for the opportunity.” I have been reading these for a YEAR now. Watching the same story play out. Marketers are asking, “Is it just me, or has marketing completely lost the plot? Is this the job I wanted? Should I just switch careers?” I even asked the same things myself. I used to love marketing. Now, I don't even know what to say. What even was marketing before all of this? Was it always like this and we are just noticing it now? Or did it get worse in the last few years? What used to be a blend of strategy and execution turned into survival mode . AI promised efficiency. Instead, it created more expectation. Faster turnarounds. More output. Tighter budgets. Leadership sees AI as a shortcut, not a tool. So the workload? It went up. Headcount? Went down. Pressure? TRIPLED. The marketer role did not evolve. It got gutted and repackaged. This article is not about the trends. Not the hype. Just focusing on the one question we all dread to be answered. How real is marketer burnout, and how did we get here? What happens when your creative energy gets consumed by meetings, client briefs, and endless edits? How do you stay motivated when everyone blames your team for poor performance but no one credits you when a campaign wins? Why do marketers, especially in digital, feel like they are always running on empty? The Modern Marketing Role is a Trap! Burnout in marketing is not new. What’s different now is how fast it spreads and how deeply it affects people across roles. From content specialists and media buyers to strategists and SEO managers, burnout is everywhere. Not because people are lazy or bad at their jobs. They are overwhelmed, underappreciated, and stuck in systems that demand more while offering less. Marketers today wear too many hats. Generalist roles stretch across brand, analytics, operations, and sales support. It used to be enough to run great creative. Now you are expected to prove ROI, optimize in real-time, adjust to AI tools, and still produce on-brand messaging across ten platforms. The second something underperforms, marketing takes the fall. But when results are good? Sales or other department will take the credit. That’s not an exaggeration. One Reddit comment I saw earlier hit it perfectly: “The sales team shouldn't be the only ones getting commission since we (content team) did all the work.” That’s the norm in many agencies and in-house teams. Marketers drive interest, create value, and nurture leads. Sales closes once the hard part is already done. There’s a word for that dynamic: exhausting . The Workload Keeps Growing Burnout is tied to more than just being busy. It’s the layoffs. The increased cost of living. The consolidation of roles. Managers freeze raises. Employees fear losing their jobs, so they overperform to avoid the next round of cuts. That creates a cycle. You take on more . You work harder . You don’t complain . And then your reward is more responsibility, not more support. Not a better salary. You become your own bottleneck. You say yes to everything because the team is small and leadership needs “just one more push.” Eventually, you hit a wall. Creativity dies. Enthusiasm fades. Work turns into survival. No Respect, No Boundaries Marketing roles are highly visible but rarely respected. Everyone thinks they can do your job. Leadership gives vague direction but expects strong positioning. Product teams shift priorities mid-sprint. Sales wants new decks with impossible turnaround times. People expect you to spin…

articles.title: I took the iPhone 18 Pro to New Zealand to find out just how good its cameras really are
articles.content: Apple has touted the addition of a variable aperture main camera on the new iPhone 18 Pro , claiming it delivers an improvement in low-light photos and video, and more control over depth of field when composing shots. But with an almost identical design and spec sheet to the excellent iPhone 17 Pro , the iPhone 18 Pro begs the question: are these camera upgrades incremental, or worth the extra investment? I received my iPhone 18 Pro review sample on September 21, two days before flying to New Zealand for a month-long trip to see family and friends. The country's dramatic scenery proved the perfect place to put the iPhone 18 Pro through its paces, and I ended up shooting more than 750 still images to see if Apple's much-hyped photography upgrades cut the mustard. In addition to that variable aperture feature, Apple also added ‘pro’ manual controls to the iPhone 18 Pro's camera app for the first time, as well as more customization options for Photographic Styles, including a film effect and film grain effect. Cumulatively, these granular control options are quite un-Apple, putting much more control in the hands of an iPhone photographer who might be used to a simpler point-and-shoot experience. In doing so, Apple is asking for its latest iPhone to be held to a higher standard. And the bottom line is that, while the iPhone 18 Pro has the best and most versatile camera setup of any iPhone to date, there are more capable alternatives available just a short hop over the tech fence in Android land for platform-agnostic mobile photographers who want the very best available. Variable aperture (Image credit: Future/Jacob Krol) The variable aperture is a physically moving mechanism that can be manually changed between four different f-stops — the smaller the f-stop number, the more light is allowed to reach the lens, and vice versa. The iPhone 18 Pro’s main camera is a 48MP sensor that can switch between f/1.4, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0. This makes it the most flexible iPhone camera lens to date, but Apple only allows those four settings — unlike a real camera, you can’t adjust to incremental f-stops between those numbers. The variable aperture in action on the iPhone 18 Pro (Image credit: Jacob Krol/Future) Changing the aperture on the iPhone 18 Pro subtly changes how much background blur a shot has when there's a subject in focus in the foreground. This is how cameras work, but usually, the small sensor on a phone requires software-enabled portrait modes to achieve this bokeh effect. The iPhone 18 Pro can do it with hardware only, though the difference between the four settings is quite minimal, as seen here: f/1.48 Future f/1.8 Future f/2.8 Future f/4.0 Future You can change the aperture manually, but it’ll also change automatically by default. And after a month of using the iPhone 18 Pro as my main camera, I feel this is still how Apple's latest flagship should be used: as a point-and-shoot camera with its default settings enabled. As you can see from many of my favorite images, the iPhone chooses the main lens at f/1.8 frequently, and it'll usually be spot on. As mentioned, this variable aperture is the headline feature of the iPhone 18 Pro, but the subtlety with which it changes the photography experience versus the iPhone 17 Pro suggests there’s not much more Apple can do with its flagship camera system. That said, the addition of customizable ‘pro’ controls within the camera app is a nice touch. I set my control panel to show shutter speed, white balance, and aperture, and they were fun to play around with to achieve better shots in low light, for instance. But unless you're invested in wringing the best possible results from the iPhone 18 Pro's lenses, you’ll likely forget about these new controls after a while. The good news is that, if you're a more casual shooter, Tap to Focus continues to work well on the iPhone 18 Pro. I was impressed with the main lens' ability to capture the two images below. articles.title: Moving from AI adoption to an AI operating model: How Docusign engineering went beyond tool rollout
articles.content: Docusign rolled out AI coding tools across its engineering teams, expecting them to help developers write code faster and do more. Initial enthusiasm was high, but early gains plateaued. By June 2025, Docusign had reached a sticking point. According to its engineering team’s account , 49% of engineers were actively using AI coding tools, while a reported 18% improvement in developer productivity had leveled off. Engineers still needed time to experiment, guidance tailored to Docusign’s codebase, and help fitting the tools into their day-to-day work. Docusign now reports that all of its more than 1,100 engineers are onboarded to and actively using AI coding tools Docusign CTO Sagnik Nandy CTO Sagnik Nandy believes getting people to use the technology is only the beginning. “There’s a big difference between trying to get a few wins versus doing it consistently and doing it right,” Nandy tells The New Stack . Docusign responded by changing how it introduced and measured AI across engineering, moving beyond coding assistants toward reusable agents and automated workflows. Why Docusign turned to its engineers Instead of making AI adoption mandatory, Docusign established a six-person Eng AI Champions team to develop guardrails, share engineering practices, and run workshops. Docusign reports that adoption reached 65% by October 2025. The company then extended that work through AI Multipliers embedded in individual development teams. Nandy says around 75 Multipliers helped teammates put the shared practices into use and fed problems back to the central team. “They were tasked with two things,” Nandy explains. “The decisions, the solutions we built, they had to deploy it within their team, and also get feedback in terms of what’s working, what’s not working, and what’s missing.” Docusign’s account of the initiative showed that active usage reached 93% within two months of introducing the Multipliers, while lines of code updated per developer increased by approximately 52% from the company’s starting point. That code-volume measure does not, by itself, establish a matching improvement in delivery speed or software quality. Nandy believes the combination of central coordination and feedback from individual teams has helped sustain the program, an approach he has also discussed in an engineering leadership podcast . “When I speak to many of my peers, a lot of AI programs start well, and then fizzle out.” “When I speak to many of my peers, a lot of AI programs start well, and then fizzle out,” he says. “I think the reason that hasn’t happened for us … is because we already have such a rich body of information and feedback flowing in, and people acting on it and then redeploying things.” Teaching AI to ‘speak Docusign’ Once engineers were comfortable using AI for coding, Docusign began looking at entire development workflows. That required tools with access to its repositories, architecture, telemetry, and internal practices, so assistants could work with the company’s own context. “Our solutions and agents, we joke, they speak Docusign,” Nandy says. “They know which internal tools to go look into, what our internal coding guardrails are, guidelines are, what system choices we make, where information resides for disambiguating between different pieces of information.” Nandy describes several internal tools for different engineering tasks: Kody for Docusign-specific coding work, Chronicle for observability and incident investigation, and DocuWiki for code-aware internal documentation. Docusign’s engineering blog also describes an AI-assisted code review tool for identifying potential architectural and security issues during review. Krew brings these capabilities together , allowing teams to build agents called Krewmates for recurring tasks and more complex…

articles.title: Netflix just added 15 shows in November 2026 — here are the top 3 with the highest scores on Rotten Tomatoes (all 92% or higher)
articles.content: Netflix’s November 2026 slate is live, and so far this month, the streamer's added a whopping 15 new shows to its library. I'd wager that’s more shows than most subscribers probably watch in a whole year — trying to finish it all in a month is basically impossible. To help you figure out what to watch first, I’ve turned to review site Rotten Tomatoes to pick out the Netflix arrivals with the highest critics' scores. Of course, just because a show has a high Rotten Tomatoes rating doesn't mean it will be to every Netflix subscriber's taste, but it's a great jumping off point to see which new-to-Netflix shows are probably worth your time. Before diving into November's top three, a quick point of order: Any Netflix originals not yet released at the time of writing were left off the list, as they lack Rotten Tomatoes scores. If two titles tied, I used the audience score to break the deadlock. With that out of the way, here are the three TV shows added to Netflix in November 2026 with the highest scores on Rotten Tomatoes. 'Bass X Machina' A badass Black protagonist in a Western steampunk anime? Sign me up. "Bass X Machina" stars Brian Tyree Henry as Bass Reeves, a real-life escaped slave turned groundbreaking lawman whose legacy inspired a Taylor Sheridan show and HBO’s “Watchmen,” among other pieces of pop culture. Showrunner LeSean Thomas ("The Boondocks," "Black Dynamite," "The Legend of Korra") uses his legacy as a jumping off point for a mesmerizing mythos all its own, blending fantastical steampunk westerns with real-life history — and it's cool as shit. In a frontier crawling with vicious outlaws, rogue machines, and supernatural nasties, Bass — whose sporting a cybernetic arm because it's sick af — has his hands full dispensing justice while keeping his family out of the crossfire. He goes on one last job in search of a missing inventor, roving a post-Civil War steampunk America with his sidekick Dana Starr (Tati Gabrielle) in tow. Even if anime isn't usually your thing, I urge you to check this one out. Rotten Tomatoes score: 100% Stream all six episodes of "Bass X Machina" on Netflix now 'North of North' season 2 For a perfect show for the dark winter months, look no further than "North of North." Set in Ice Cove, Nunavut, this breezy sitcom unfolds in Canada's northernmost territory, where there's no shortage of daylight. Season 2 sees Anna Lambe return as Siaja, a young mother still finding her footing after divorcing the town's golden boy. This season, she's ready to give romance another shot, and dives headfirst into the chilly waters of the speed-dating scene. Community remains at the heart of the show as Siaja tries to reconnect with her dad (Jay Ryan) and track down her biological sister. Also throwing a wrench in the works is her new boss, Helen (Mary Lynn Rajskub, aka the unforgettable Chloe from "24"). "North of North" is an easygoing comedy with plenty of heart, some seriously gorgeous scenery, and enough low-stakes drama to keep the pace moving along. Rotten Tomatoes score: 100% Stream both seasons of "North of North" on Netflix now 'Black Doves' season 2 For a more high-octane wintry watch, Keira Knightley is back as the fan-favorite spy-for-hire Helen in season 2 of "Black Doves." Still feeding government secrets to the covert organization Black Doves, and with her husband, Wallace (Andrew Buchan), set to become U.K. prime minister, she teams up with her old friend, Sam (Ben Whishaw), for an even more dangerous mission. When her handler, Mrs. Reed, (Sarah Lancashire), is accused of plotting a coup against the organization, it unearths some fascinating revelations about her past, including a family a connection that proves more deadly than anyone expected. There's plenty of twists and sharp dialogue to keep you invested, but the real appeal comes from Whishaw and Knightley, whose genuine chemistry with one another shines through all the shoot outs and drama you'd expect from a spy thriller. articles.title: iOS Startup Performance in Practice, Part 2: Measuring App Launch Time in Production
articles.content: How to measure startup on real user devices, define trustworthy production percentiles, and use XCTest and Instruments to explain regressions. The easiest way to measure app launch time is to start a stopwatch, open the app, and write down the number. It is also one of the easiest ways to produce a measurement that cannot be reproduced, compared, or trusted. An iOS launch depends on more than the code in the repository. The result changes with the process state, system caches, device model, thermal state, available memory, network behavior, stored user data, app version, and the destination the user is trying to open. Two measurements can both be technically correct while describing different experiences. In Part 1 , we separated cold launch, warm launch, resume, scene creation, and entry points. We also defined three possible endpoints: First Draw, Meaningful Content, and Time to Interactive. Now we can turn that model into a measurement system. This article is the second part of iOS Startup Performance in Practice , a six-part series: Understanding Launch Types and Entry Points Measuring App Launch Time Correctly Finding Bottlenecks from dyld to the First Frame Designing a Scalable Startup Architecture From the First Frame to an Interactive UI Preventing Regressions in Production The goal of this part is not to find a single perfect number. It is to build a production measurement system that describes what real users experience - and then use controlled tests and profiling to explain why that distribution changes. A launch number is meaningless without a measurement contract Suppose one engineer reports a launch time of 1.4 seconds and another reports 2.1 seconds. Before comparing them, we need to know: Did both tests create a new process? Were they cold or warm launches? Was the app opened from the icon or through a link? Did the timer stop at First Draw or when the screen became interactive? Did both runs use the same device and OS version? Was the debugger attached? Did both users have the same local data and authentication state? Was the network real, disabled, or stubbed? Without these answers, the numbers are labels rather than evidence. Let’s start with production metrics. For every launch metric, define a measurement contract : Dimension Example value Population Real user launches of app version `8.24.0` Launch class New-process launch; resume reported separately Entry point Icon, link, notification, and quick action segmented where custom telemetry allows it Start boundary System launch start for MetricKit; first application marker for custom metrics End boundary First Draw for the system metric; Home Interactive for the product metric User segments Signed-out and authenticated users reported separately Technical segments Device performance tier, iOS version, app version, and migration state Aggregation window Seven complete days after the target rollout reaches a stable cohort Reported values Every sample, median, p90, and maximum Data source MetricKit or Organizer for system launch; custom telemetry for product milestones Exclusions Internal builds, synthetic runs, invalid or incomplete milestone sequences This table describes measurement on user devices. There are no fixed test phones, stubbed networks, or XCTest iterations in the production contract. Real device and network diversity are not noise to remove; they are part of the experience we are trying to understand. The first rule of launch measurement is therefore: Define the population and user-visible endpoint before naming the number. Instead of writing “launch time is 1.8 seconds,” write: For production new-process launches of version 8.24.x, Time to First Draw is 1.1 seconds at p50 and 1.8 seconds at p90 across 2.4 million samples. Authenticated users on the lowest device tier have a p90 of 2.6 seconds. The values are illustrative, but the form is important: it tells us who experienced the delay, which boundary was measured, and whether the percentile…

articles.title: Building Reliable iOS Apps With AI Agents
articles.content: One year ago I wrote Breaking Free from Xcode: Unlock AI's Full Potential in iOS . At that time, getting an agent to build, run and check an iOS app took a pile of MCP servers, VS Code extensions and some patience. A lot has changed since. Models are much smarter. Xcode ships with agents built in. Claude Code can control the simulator on its own: it builds, launches, taps through screens and checks the result with screenshots. So, is iOS development solved? For prototypes and MVPs , mostly yes. You can describe an idea and get the app “one-shotted”. But if your software has to be as reliable as running water (a phrase I borrow from Uber's mission : "transportation as reliable as running water, everywhere, for everyone"), two principles still matter: design and harness . Principle 1: You still own the design This is the biggest shift I've seen. While building a feature, I don't keep in my head which method calls which method, which file it lives in, or how state moves through each type. The agent handles that. That doesn't mean you can stop reviewing code. Where quality matters, you still read PRs. But your attention moves up a level. You own the design of the whole system , not just one module, so architecture is now the most valuable skill you have. At the design level you are pretty high in the hierarchy of components, that’s why visualization helps. A diagram with the right amount of detail shows how the pieces fit together, which is hard to see in plain text. The C4 model gives you that visualization at a few zoom levels. Last year I suggested putting the project architecture in AGENTS.md . I've changed my mind: a dedicated docs/architecture/ folder is a better place. You don't need the entire architecture loaded into the context every time you do something. Instead, AGENTS.md keeps a reference to docs/architecture/context.md , so the agent can retrieve it when on demand. Luis Herrera's deep dive walks through C4 levels on a sample system. System Context. Your app, its users and the outside systems it talks to: the backend, push notifications, analytics. This is context.md , and it links to the containers. Containers. Conventional C4 container usually stands for a piece of software that can de deployed, like a micro-service or app. I had to adapt the original idea: a container is a feature, a flow or an SDK module, like Feed, Checkout or Networking. containers.md shows how they connect, explains what each one owns and what it may depend on, and links to components where they exist. Components. The parts inside a container. Only draw these for complex areas , like a post composer with drafts, uploads and retries, or a sync engine. A stateless FeedService with a single getFeed() call doesn't need a component diagram. C4 itself says you only need the levels "that add value". Code. No diagrams. Component docs just link to the specific files. The code is the source of truth, and an agent can read it faster than you can draw it. Think about C4 as a pattern that generalizes an approach to structure progressive complexity of the architecture. Here's what that looks like for a simple feed app: AGENTS.md ← rules + link to context.md docs/architecture/ context.md ← system context, links to containers.md containers.md ← container diagram, links to components components/composer.md ← complex flow only, links to code Here's the container diagram from containers.md , as Mermaid source and rendered: Use Mermaid. It's plain text, so it shows up in diffs, GitHub renders it, and agents read it as easily as code. This is what I call discoverable architecture . The agent doesn't load the whole architecture up front. AGENTS.md points it to context.md , and from there it follows links down only as far as the task needs. Humans onboard the same way. Keep the diagrams alive Documentation that goes stale is worse than none. So let the agent maintain it: Add a skill that updates the affected docs and diagrams in docs/architecture/ after a change. articles.title: Norwegians Release FOSS GNOME Software for Music Recording, Internet Radio, and Cameras
articles.content: ole (Slashdot reader #19,909) writes in about his free, Norwegian open-source music recording studio for GNOME called GarageJam, which he says allows musicians to compose, record, and share original music seamlessly on the Internet. The latest release, GarageJam 8.0.1, is available in C and Python. It records audio immediately to Ogg Vorbis (.ogg) files in the current working directory and lets you edit metadata in .gjxml XML files from a GTK/GNOME wizard — all built on the Gingerblue Recording Studio API. Ole shares links to its IETF GarageJam XML draft and GitHub repositories, and there's also GarageJam Studio, "a commercial music and audio recording app for the World Wide Web written by Aamot Innovation from Norway.". ole is also spreading the word about GNOME Media, which "puts internet radio and your photographs on one OpenStreetMap... built from GNOME Radio 85.0.1." Click a station on the map to listen. Cities with several stations show a count and a menu. Open a folder of pictures or import from a camera. Photos with a GPS position in their EXIF data appear on the map. Double-click a thumbnail to open it. The search box filters the station list and the map together. ole also announces: GPhoto 3.0.1. ("After 25 years, libgphoto2 2.5.34 now supports more than 2,500 camera models, and GPhoto 3.0.1 is built on it.") Skolelinux 13.6.0. Built on Debian 13 âoetrixieâ, Skolelinux is "a complete, ready-to-use Free Software operating system for schools, classrooms and home computers... an office suite, web browser, educational programs and network services for an entire school, all set up out of the box." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Scaling an autonomous agent from one team to fifty: A serverless-to-container decision framework
articles.content: QA teams shipping complex products generate test failures around the clock. Every failure needs a bug ticket with steps, screenshots, repro rates, and regression labels. The manual process takes 10-15 minutes per failure. Multiply that by 30+ failures per week across a team, and you have burned an entire engineering day on documentation that should be automatic. I built a system to eliminate this entirely. Not a dashboard. Not a notification bot. An autonomous agent that observes test results, makes judgment calls – is this a new bug, a duplicate, or a regression? And takes action without human intervention. It files structured bugs, attaches screenshots, calculates repro rates, detects regressions build-over-build, and notifies the right people. The team just marks FAIL and moves on. The system runs on Lambda today. It works perfectly for one team. But what happens when other teams want it? What happens when you need to serve 10, 50, or 100 teams? That’s where the architectural decisions get interesting – not because Lambda fails, but because the workload characteristics shift into territory where a different tool becomes the better fit. What I built (and why it works) The architecture is elegant: an EventBridge rule triggers a Lambda function every 15 minutes. The function polls the test management API, processes failures through a decision engine (dedup check against DynamoDB, regression detection against previous build results), and files bugs via the JIRA API. Total infrastructure cost: under $5/month. Lambda was the correct choice here for three reasons: Zero operational overhead: No servers, no scaling config, no patching. Deploy and forget. Cost proportional to usage: One team generates ~200 invocations/month. At Lambda pricing, this is effectively free. Fast iteration: The decision engine went through 20+ revisions in the first month. Lambda’s deployment model let me ship changes in seconds. Within weeks of deploying, the system filed more complete and consistent bugs than the team had ever produced manually. Zero missed failures. Regressions caught in minutes instead of days. Status interruptions to QA dropped to zero because anyone could query the system directly via Slack. 8-10 hours per week saved. Other teams have noticed. “Can we have that?” is a recurring question. The answer seems simple – deploy another instance per team. But at scale, the workload characteristics change in ways that shift the architectural decision. The scaling decision Lambda handles single-tenant agentic workloads beautifully. The challenge at multi-tenant scale isn’t that Lambda can’t do it; it’s that the workload characteristics shift: From stateless events to long-running context: A single team’s poll cycle finishes in seconds. But cross-project correlation – “is this the same failure pattern we’re seeing across three teams?” requires analyzing hundreds of results and their relationships in a single pass. That’s a fundamentally different compute profile. From isolated invocations to shared resource contention: When 50 functions trigger on the same EventBridge schedule, they all hit TestRail and JIRA APIs simultaneously. You need centralized rate limiting, connection pooling, and backpressure – patterns that benefit from persistent, shared infrastructure. From single-team to multi-tenant isolation: Each team needs guaranteed resources, network boundaries, and scoped credentials. The isolation model becomes as important as the compute model. Lambda’s recent launches address many of these individually – Managed Instances solve connection persistence, Durable Functions break the 15-minute ceiling for long-running workflows, and Tenant Isolation provides native tenant boundaries. For many multi-tenant workloads, these capabilities narrow the gap significantly. But for this specific workload – long-running agents that need persistent connections, cross-tenant analysis, GPU inference, and namespace-level isolation simultaneously- the decision…

articles.title: 19 Agent Skills Test Your Web App With Playwright and Real Browsers
articles.content: Nineteen open-licensed agent skills let an AI agent test a web app the way a person would: write the test first, open a real browser, click through the flows and report what broke. They come from Vercel Labs' agent-browser , Tech Leads Club , Anthropic , Matt Pocock, Jesse Vincent and lackeyjb . All 19 are packaged as the QA & Testing plugin in Cuttlefish.MD , HackerNoon's license-checked skills marketplace. They follow the open Agent Skills standard , so they run in Claude Code, Codex CLI and 30+ other tools , and each is indexed in HackerNoon's SKILL.md Library . The 19 QA and testing skills Skill What it does Author agent-browser A browser automation CLI built for AI agents Vercel Labs agentcore Runs agent-browser on AWS Bedrock AgentCore cloud browsers Vercel Labs chrome-devtools Debugs, profiles and automates the browser through the Chrome DevTools MCP server Tech Leads Club core The core agent-browser usage guide Vercel Labs demo Records a demo video of a feature on a real desktop with a real cursor Tech Leads Club derive-client Records browser traffic to reverse-engineer a site's internal API and generate a client Vercel Labs dogfood Explores a web app systematically to find bugs and UX problems Vercel Labs electron Automates Electron desktop apps such as VS Code, Slack and Figma Vercel Labs playwright-skill Full browser automation with Playwright lackeyjb playwright-skill Tech Leads Club's packaging of Playwright browser automation Tech Leads Club protected-vercel-deployments Tests Vercel deployments behind SSO or Deployment Protection Vercel Labs slack Works in Slack workspaces through browser automation Vercel Labs spec-driven-eval Grades how completely an implementation meets its PRD, case by case Tech Leads Club tdd Builds features and fixes bugs test-first, red-green-refactor Matt Pocock test-driven-development Writes the failing test before any implementation code Jesse Vincent tlc-spec-driven Plans and builds features in four phases: specify, design, tasks, execute Tech Leads Club vercel-sandbox Runs agent-browser and Chrome inside Vercel Sandbox microVMs Vercel Labs webapp-testing Tests local web apps with Playwright Anthropic webmcp-gen Builds and validates experimental WebMCP tools for a page Vercel Labs Install all 19 in one command /plugin marketplace add hackernoon/cuttlefish-agent-skills /plugin install qa-testing@cuttlefish For Codex CLI, Cursor or another agent that supports the standard, clone the repo and copy plugins/qa-testing/skills/ into your agent's skills folder, such as .agents/skills/ . The agent-browser skills need Vercel's agent-browser CLI installed. Each skill keeps its license and an ATTRIBUTION.md naming its author and source commit. Browse the full library at hackernoon.com/skills , and star Cuttlefish.MD on GitHub .

articles.title: Apple’s M5 MacBook Air is down to its lowest price since July
articles.content: A top-down view of the 15-inch MacBook Air, which features Apple’s M5 processor. | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge The latest 13-inch MacBook Air is currently available for $1,099.99, marking the second time we’ve seen this $200 discount following the company’s hefty price increases over the summer . Although the base model — which features Apple’s M5 processor, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage — often sold for around $950 to $1,000 shortly after it launched in May, savings have been rare since July, making the current deal worth flagging. Amazon , Best Buy , and B&H Photo are all honoring the price across all color options. If you’d prefer something with a larger screen, a six-speaker array instead of four, and slightly more power (with two additional GPU cores in the M5), Apple’s 15-inch MacBook Air is also on sale for $200 off. Amazon , Best Buy , and B&H Photo are each selling the 16GB RAM / 512GB SSD configuration in most colors for $1,299.99. Apple 13-inch MacBook Air (M5) Where to Buy: $1299 $1099 at Amazon $1299 $1099 at Best Buy $1299 $1099 at B&H Photo Although it’s pricier than the newer MacBook Neo, the Air offers better value in numerous ways. It’s an ideal choice if you want faster performance, as it offers double the RAM and a speedier CPU with more cores. You also get twice as much storage, better speakers, a backlit keyboard, and a larger, higher-resolution screen. Given said differences, it’s easy to see how the Air’s improvements might make it worth the extra cost for some people. If you’re still on the fence, though, I’d recommend reading my colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto’s reviews, both of which were published before the summer price increases. Read our full MacBook Neo and M5 MacBook Air reviews.

articles.title: Apple Taking New Approach to Developing iOS 28 and macOS 28
articles.content: Apple has made a change to its development process for iOS 28, macOS 28, and corresponding software updates, according to Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman. In his Power On newsletter today , he said Apple separates development of each year's new operating systems into three major stages. Typically, he said each stage consists of four weeks of coding followed by a four-week "convergence" period where new features are integrated into the operating systems. This time around, Apple has made a change. The first stage of development for iOS 28 and the other updates apparently consisted of six weeks of coding and two weeks of feature convergence. This change gives Apple's software engineers more time to come up with new features. "Instead of the normal split between two four-week efforts, Apple engineers were tasked with six weeks of coding, exploration and feature development, and then only two weeks of convergence," he said. "Employees say they like the change, indicating that it creates more time for coming up with ideas and exploring them before needing to lock things in." Gurman did not reveal any specific features planned for iOS 28. The update should be available in beta in June and released in September next year. articles.title: Python's CVEs Triple. Anthropic Funds a New Security Developer
articles.content: In the last year CVEs have increased 3x for Python and its package manager Pip, according to Python's security developer in residence Seth Larson. "And the amount of malware published and removed from the Python Package Index (PyPI) is up 60%." Securing Python's ecosystem is getting more complex, he writes, especially given "the evolving role of AI in both security risks and security response." Their response includes bringing on a new Security Developer "to address the increasingly demanding scale of security response for the Python ecosystem." Providing prompt security response services and innovating to prevent future threats... is more difficult now than ever before... [Security developer Brett Smith] will help us keep pace with critical ongoing work such as vulnerability remediation, providing vulnerability data as a CVE Numbering Authority, and removing malware from PyPI. He'll also give the team bandwidth for new projects such as scaling PyPI's autonomous quarantine program to reduce manual effort on malware remediation and streamlining processes for the PSRT to handle the new vulnerability report volume. The role was made possible by an "ecosystem security" grant from Anthropic. And having the new security developer "will both build capacity for security work the PSF already does and enable new, proactive work," concludes Python's security developer in residence. (He discussed Python's security challenges in a June presentation with Python security engineer Mike Fiedler> .) In June, Curl's Daniel Strenberg reported Curl's CVEs have also tripled.
