articles.title: Perplexity’s AI agents keep working after you close the tab
articles.content: Perplexity’s new Teammates can coordinate multiple agents, remember where previous sessions left off, and keep working without another prompt. The challenge is keeping everything in sync, especially when agents are working at the same time, sharing project state, and operating with different permissions. Announced Wednesday , Teammates builds on infrastructure Perplexity has spent much of the year developing. The launch puts that earlier work to use in workflows where agents can delegate tasks and continue operating across sessions. The challenge of keeping agents stateful When Nate Kupp , Perplexity’s vice president of infrastructure, took The New Stack inside the company’s agent sandboxes , he described the difficulty of maintaining reliable systems at that scale. “Stateful systems are incredibly hard to build,” Kupp said, pointing to the durability and uptime requirements of operating millions of sandboxes. “Stateful systems are incredibly hard to build” Teammates relies on Perplexity Computer’s existing infrastructure, which separates persistent project state from individual execution environments. That allows agents to continue working on the same project without depending on a single uninterrupted session. Shared state lives in Git In a technical breakdown of its shared workspaces , the company described how it uses Git-backed repositories to keep project state intact across sessions. Each Computer project has its own repository, while agents work in separate sandboxes and submit their changes back to the shared project. That gets more complicated when agents are working on the same code at once since if one agent commits its changes first, another may have to reapply its work against the latest version. Perplexity says fewer than 2% of submissions are rejected because they’re based on outdated repository state. Median submission latency is under 1.7 seconds, while p99 stays below eight seconds. Median submission latency is under 1.7 seconds, while p99 stays below eight seconds. Memory is handled separately through Perplexity’s Brain system, which keeps what agents have learned in dedicated repositories. That lets background agents update shared knowledge without interfering with changes to the project’s files. Pausing and forking agents Perplexity built SPACE around Firecracker microVMs and Btrfs snapshots, making it possible to pause, resume, or fork agent sessions without losing their saved state. With Teammates, developers can connect tools like Slack and GitHub and set up triggers that tell agents when to act. Perplexity hasn’t said much about what happens when that work gets stuck, particularly when one agent is waiting on another or acting on information that’s already out of date. The open permission questions Each teammate runs in its own isolated environment and browser session, with access managed through Computer’s existing permissions and credentials handled securely through encryption. Users can also monitor progress and take control when needed. It’s unclear how it prevents agents from accessing resources beyond their permissions when tasks are handed off. For enterprises, that uncertainty could influence how much autonomy they’re willing to give agents without requiring human approval. Teammates is initially available on the web for Perplexity Max subscribers, with iOS support planned. articles.title: Diamond Foundry creates world's first 200mm single-crystal diamond wafer
articles.content: Diamonds have exceptional cooling capabilities due to their excellent thermal conductivity, with the material estimated to be at least five times more conductive than copper . Because of this, Diamond Foundry, a firm focusing on lab-grown diamonds, announced the world’s first 200mm single-crystal diamond (SCD) wafer. The 200mm SCD is about the same wafer size that semiconductor fabs use for older processes, with the company boasting on its website that “Single-crystal diamond has entered the wafer-scale era.” This is part of the effort to manufacture SCD at scale so that it can be used for semiconductor cooling, especially now that increasing power of AI chips has also led to enormous thermal problems. What makes Diamond Foundry’s 200mm SCD wafer different from other lab-grown diamonds is that it’s created as a high-quality single-crystal piece instead of a polycrystalline gem. Although the former is difficult to manufacture, it is what allows diamond to become an extreme efficient thermal conductor while simultaneously retaining its electrical insulating properties — this efficiency should help cut down on hotspots, making SCDs an excellent solution for AI chip cooling. The company also showed in a graph that it is now thought possible to create a D300 SCD wafer before 2030, matching the size of the wafers used in leading node processes. However, it should be noted that the sample shown by the company remains unpolished, meaning it still needs to go through some processes to make it suitable for chipmakers. (Image credit: Diamond Foundry ) Although the company was founded in 2012, it also acknowledged the work of scientists who have been chipping away at the scale problem of SCDs since the early 2000s. “This is one of those milestones that once seemed almost impossible. Hundreds of DF engineers, scientists, and technicians contributed to us getting here. It is the accumulated result of countless experiments, failures, inventions, rebuilt machines, and insights over more than a decade,” Diamond Foundry CEO Martin Roscheisen said. “Stefan and Martin pursued this goal for 25 years. There are very few examples in technology of someone sticking to a really hard scientific challenge with that level of perseverance. They kept going when the prevailing view was that single‑crystal diamond simply could not be made at this scale. Today, the perseverance shows as the first-ever D200mm single‑crystal diamond. And best of all, it makes D300mm predictable as well.” Diamond Foundry Diamond Foundry Diamond Foundry isn’t the only company that has identified the potential of lab-grown diamonds for semiconductor cooling. Akash Systems secured $18.2 million in CHIPS Act funding in 2024 to produce Gallium Nitride fused with synthetic diamond , which it claims will reduce temperatures by 20 degrees C. The De Beers Group, which is known for its diamond mines in Africa, is also building a copper-plated diamond composite material aimed at improving cooling efficiency for AI, high-performance computing, and GaN RF devices. Even Frore Systems, which is known for its solid-state cooler , is diving into diamond-infused watercooling cold plates for Nvidia’s next-generation AI GPUs.

articles.title: Logitech G502 X Lightspeed Review: No lights, same price
articles.content: Logitech's G502 X Lightspeed has been around for awhile — the mouse was introduced in 2022 alongside the fancier Logitech G502 X Plus (and the wired G502 X), but since it’s receiving a firmware update that upgrades its Hero 25K sensor to a Hero 44K sensor, this seemed like a good time to take a look at it. The G502X Lightspeed is available in black and white colorways and currently retails for $159.99, which is the same price as the G502 X Plus — however, it can (and should) normally be found for less than this. Design and Comfort of the G502 X Lightspeed The Logitech G502 X Lightspeed is a right-handed gaming mouse with an ergonomically contoured shape. It's the same size and shape as the G502 X Plus, with large primary mouse buttons, textured rubber side panels for grip, and a smooth matte chassis with glossy accents. It comes in black and white colorways (our review unit was black) and has no lighting aside from a small indicator light at the front of the mouse to indicate connection and battery life. Like the G502 X Plus, the G502 X Lightspeed is definitely on the larger side. It measures 5.17 inches (131.4mm) long by 3.12 inches (79.2mm) wide, and is 1.62 inches (41.1mm) high at its tallest point. It's larger than the Razer Basilisk V3 Pro and V4 Pro (5.11 x 2.96 x 1.67 inches / 130 x 75.4 x 42.5mm) — not by a lot, but it definitely feels like a much larger mouse. It weighs about 3.6 ounces (102g), which makes it lighter than the Basilisk V3 Pro, but slightly heavier than the Basilisk V4 Pro. Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware The G502 X Lightspeed has 11 programmable buttons, and 13 programmable controls if you include scroll up/down. There are the left and right primary mouse buttons, as well as two side buttons along the left edge of the left mouse button. On the left side of the mouse there are the two standard thumb buttons, plus a "sniper" button that's magnetically attached and can be flipped so that it's not in your way. The sniper button can also be "deleted," and Logitech includes a delete cover in the box that makes the button unpressable (and also has the same soft, rubbery texture as the rest of the thumb rest). articles.title: Japanese arcades suffer week-long blackout following Sega server hack
articles.content: The sensory overload typically experienced when visiting video game arcades in Japan was eerily absent from some venues this week, reports ITMedia News [machine translation]. It says that a Sega system outage meant there was “no end in sight” for the rows of silent black screens. However, a recent tweet from arcade network operator ALL.net indicates that both Sega and Bandai Namco machines are affected. Moreover, arcade lovers will be pleased to hear that affected arcades will “gradually resume operation on a trial basis starting today.” a friend sent me some pics of their local arcade and LMAO the sega outage is nuts https://t.co/3vSYjCYAIZ November 3, 2026 ALL.Net, a contraction of Amusement Linkage Live Network, was launched by Sega in 2004 to allow arcade games to look up to the net for auto updates, data logging, implement online play, and power national leaderboards. Sega titles like Initial D The Arcade, Maimai, and CHUNITHM , rely on this network, as do Bandai Namco games like A iko no Tatsujin, Mario Kart Arcade GP DX, and Gundam Extreme Vs . Some services are gradually resuming operation today. (Image credit: ALL.Net, Sega Fave ) In its official apology blog post, dated November 2, ALL.Net / Sega Fave said that it suspended services a day prior after it became aware of its servers being affected by “unauthorized access by a third party.” It reassured customers that their personal info and billing data were not on the compromised server. However, it asked for more time to investigate, run safety checks, and so on, before restoring service. This morning ALL.Net told customers that Bandia Namco titles “will gradually resume operation on a trial basis starting today (online play and card use enabled).” Sega products remain under maintenance, and online services are unavailable. There is currently no estimate for issue resolution, but a news bulletin is promised for November 10 (Tuesday). Classic offline arcade machines weren’t affected by this outage, of course. Moreover, rival arcade gaming legends like Taito and Konami run their own, separate, arcade networks and authentication systems.

articles.title: The end of an era as Linux 7.5 purges the last 30-year-old Intel MMX optimizations from Pentium age
articles.content: Linux developers are preparing to make Intel’s ancient MultiMedia eXtensions an irrelevance. Intel introduced MMX in the Pentium era, but a patch expected to merge into mainline Linux 7.5 will remove the last remaining optimized software from the open-source OS. Expected to be released in 2027, the new kernel will wipe MMX-optimized code from its software RAID XOR code, explains Phoronix . Admittedly, there wasn’t much left in Linux in terms of MMX optimizations. But few folks will be running the most modern kernels on Pentium MMX and Pentium II chips in 2026. And most other MMX-optimized code disappeared from the OS half a decade ago, when some MMX-optimized memory management code was removed. Note that, if you are a determined late-90s Pentium devotee, you can still use software RAID, but it will lack the MMX fast path. This is a classic case of Linux code housekeeping. With this change, the kernel will lose over 800 lines of code and replace them with just 12. Remembering MMX Intel first introduced MMX Pentium chips in January 1997. Though I vaguely remember these processors being marketed as being enhanced by ‘MultiMedia eXtensions,’ Wikipedia insists that “MMX is officially a meaningless initialism[6] trademarked by Intel.” In a subsequent trademark battle with longtime foe AMD, a document produced in court indicated that MMX stood for ‘Matrix Math Extensions.’ AMD relied on this to sidestep the trademark, as an initialism cannot be trademarked, according to the encyclopedic source. Eventually, all rival x86 processors managed to integrate MMX instructions – so as not to be pushed into the shade during the multimedia boom. A surprisingly large number of non-Intel chips ended up offering MMX, too. Along with Pentium MMX chips, AMD, Centaur, Cyrix , Rise, and Transmeta eventually offered MMX CPUs. After MMX's marketing success, AMD pioneered 3DNow! instructions , and about a year later, Intel fired back with SSE and SSE2.

articles.title: Ukraine builds combat robots to hunt Russian troops in underground gas pipelines
articles.content: Ukraine is developing a new class of combat robots designed to operate inside underground gas pipelines, where Russian troops have repeatedly attempted to bypass frontline defenses, United24Media reports. The project, disclosed by Ukraine's 2 nd National Guard Corps, Khartiia, involves modifying unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) to perform reconnaissance and combat missions in spaces too narrow for conventional military machinery. Notably, the work is being carried out by specialists from the corps’ Lava Unmanned Systems Regiment, following Operation Veles — an underground assault that saw Ukrainian soldiers advance more than 15 kilometers through pipeline infrastructure near Kupiansk. Khartiia says the operation killed more than 100 enemy soldiers and resulted in over 30 captured, although those battlefield figures have not been independently verified. The commander of Lavas ground robotic system battalion, identified by the callsign ‘Matematyk’, said the project addresses a category of warfare that requires a different approach from conventional battlefield robotics. “There is a very long list of tasks that need to be accomplished to fight underground and counter the enemy underground. This is a new class of technologies and challenges that we will have to confront,” he said. The machines are being adapted from existing groundrobots ,rather than developed as conventional surface vehicles. They must be compact enough to navigate narrow pipelines while retaining the ability to carry out military assignments . Most commercially available underground machinery, meanwhile, is designed for construction, drilling, and tunneling — not combat. As of now, Khartiia is already developing several robotic systems to address those limitations, with the broader objective of sending machines into dangerous underground environments where soldiers would otherwise have to conduct reconnaissance, confront enemy positions, clear positions, or clear out themselves. “War is already underground, and it will expand. The question is how we adapt to this war,” Matematyk said. The project follows unusual battlefield developments near Kupiansk, where Ukrainian forces used the same underground infrastructure that Russian troops have previously exploited to infiltrate behind Ukrainian defensive positions. During Operation Vels, Ukrainian soldiers moved through a gas pipeline measuring approximately 1.2 meters in diameter, according to a report by Ikrainska Pravda. The confined passage made movement and close-range firefights particularly,with Ukrainian troops having little-to-no room to maneuver. Russia had previously used the pipeline network beneath the Oskil River to move soldiers toward Ukrainian-held territory. The Ukrainian battlefield monitoring group ‘Deepstate' reported an earlier Russian infiltration attempt in September 2025. Last month, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukrainian forces had eliminated more than 100 Russian troops and captured over 30 during the operation. The experience also exposed the limitation of sending soldiers into such environments. Underground operations restrict visibility,complicate communications , and leave little room for maneuvering equipment. That said, Ukraine has increased its reliance on unmanned military systems as battlefield terrain proves complicated to navigate. In July 2024, we reported on Ukrainian forces deploying AI-controlled drones capable of independently identifying and attaching targets. The country has also been experimenting with unmanned systems that operate beyond conventional aerial platforms. In August, the US Army tested an autonomous Ford F-250 breaching vehicle , which builds on the Lancer unmanned ground vehicle program and uses a counter-drone turret to protect military operations from aerial attacks. However, autonomous ground systems still face considerable technical challenges. Russia's Shturm uncrewed assault tanks , for instance , repeatedly lost their command connection…

articles.title: How Apple's Personal Knowledge Graph learns about your life on Mac
articles.content: A breakdown of Apple's Personal Knowledge Graph shows what your Mac and Apple Intelligence know about you and your life. An example of contextual Siri on Mac The upgrade to Siri AI added the understanding of personal context to Apple Intelligence . By pulling information from messages, emails, and photos, Siri can come up with answers to queries with contextual elements, such as knowing the name of your mother from a travel itinerary. However, Apple has been compiling data on its users for a lot longer, with macOS 13 doing so since 2022. In a breakdown by security researchers at Eighth Rank, the generation of a Personal Knowledge Graph in macOS is detailed, including the kinds of data it compiles and retains on your Mac. articles.title: Nvidia released its 8800 GTX GPU 20 years ago today, celebrates with Steam game homage
articles.content: On this day in 2006, Nvidia released the legendary GeForce 8800 GTX and 8800 GTS graphics cards . Nvidia has decided to honor the flagship of the pair with its GeForce 8800 GTX - 20 Years of a Legend interactive demo, now free on Steam . However, the recommended specs to ‘play’ with this semi-interactive path-traced unboxing experience include a wallet-worrying RTX 5080 . Or you could just watch the video, embedded below for your convenience. The downloadable demo, which also requires 32GB of RAM and 30GB of free storage, was created by Dylan Browne, a senior special effects artist who frequently works with Unreal Engine , as in this case. This experience is said to deliver era-appropriate graphics, but requires the most advanced graphics tech available two decades after the 8800 GTX first hit the scene to work its graphical magic. To run GeForce 8800 GTX - 20 Years of a Legend on a 2026 PC, you will need at least an RTX 4070 for acceptable performance, according to the Steam page. This software is stuffed with the latest graphics tech embraced by the green team. “DLSS 4.5 with Dynamic Multi Frame Generation, Ray Reconstruction, path tracing, and Mega Geometry” are all present, says Nvidia. Nvidia, Steam, Dylan Browne Nvidia, Steam, Dylan Browne Nvidia, Steam, Dylan Browne There’s a bit more to the interactive demo than looking around and poking a box with your mouse and then prodding it to fit the shiny new GPU into your “era-accurate PC tower.” An extra layer of fun is promised by the provision of hidden Easter eggs in this experience. However, the demo appears to show Windows Vista on the PC in the gaming den, which launched at retail a few months after the 8800 GTX. Admittedly, this legendary GeForce card and Windows Vista OS would roam the Earth at the same time, with many folks buying the GeForce 8800 GTX and 8800 GTS to shove into their Vista PCs from 2007 onwards. Crysis launched on PCs in late 2007, a year after the G80 architecture cards debuted. Nvidia launched the GeForce 8800 GTX (128 shader units) and 8800 GTS (96 shader units) at $599 and $449, respectively. These legendary Nvidia GPUs spearheaded the DirectX 10 era, accelerating existing PC titles and delivering next-gen visuals with new DX10 software. You can read more in our reviews from the time, like the 12-page review of the GeForce 8800 GTX and GTS from the launch week. Briefly, our reviewer thought these cards were “amazing” for their current performance and DX10 promise . They were also excited about the G80 architecture for bringing CUDA to consumers and the promise of making the GPU “something much more than a frame rendering device.” Some Luddite gamers may wish that had never happened. Future Future Nvidia driver support for the GeForce 8800 GTX and GTS would run out of road about a decade later. By that time, DirectX 11 hardware and games were mainstream, leaving older graphics hardware designs obsolete when it came to playing the latest AAA PC titles.

articles.title: Open-source GPU task manager reveals exactly what's eating your VRAM
articles.content: Microsoft VP Scott Hanselman has revealed a new open-source GitHub project called gputaskman . The name neatly encapsulates the headline role of this tool, a GPU-focused task manager, but its scope might be broader than you expect. This new tool for Windows, Linux, and macOS can show per-process GPU usage, VRAM consumption , active runtimes, and many more stats. It also breaks out AI/LLM task-specific information. There's a lot going on in my GPU. I'm making a GPU Taskman to get insights to where my GPU memory is going. PRs welcome https://t.co/6FwKqnFWDW November 3, 2026 On social media, Hanselman snappily makes clear the technical itch that gputaskman was designed to scratch. “There's a lot going on in my GPU,” wrote the prominent public face of Microsoft's developer ecosystem. “I'm making a GPU Taskman to get insights to where my GPU memory is going.” There are several example screenshots of GPU Taskman in use by the Microsoft VP. They clearly show the kinds of data that are presented in the terminal-like display that pops up in the tool. Hanselman’s tweet shows that the most VRAM-hungry app on his RTX 4080S system is the desktop windows manager. That is selected in the list, and more details are shown for this task at the bottom of the window. Also, we see AI/LLM apps consuming VRAM, and a few Windows staples. Looking closer at llama-server.exe (Image credit: gputaskman on GitHub ) In a GitHub-embedded image, we see what details are broken out when the llama-server.exe app is selected in the list. The bottom of the window breakdown reveals that Qwen3-0.6B is being used, and there’s a breakdown of its weights, the KV cache , the number of parameters, and more. Very informative. As the Microsoft developer has made portable Windows downloads of the latest v0.3.0 release of gputaskman, I couldn’t resist giving it a spin. Upon launch, I found that no tasks were using the discrete GPU in my laptop… so I fired up ye olde Unigine Valley GPU benchmark to stir the RTX 4060 from its slumber. I note the live-streaming charts showing GPU load, VRAM use, temperature, and so on are more prominent in my screenshot than in Hanselman’s examples. Perhaps he screen-shotted a previous version of the tool. Valley's GPU resource use (Image credit: Future) There’s a lot more information about gputaskman, its inner workings, and even its source code, on the linked GitHub repository. Hanselman is sharing his “experimental software” tool under the permissive MIT license. Finally, in social media comments, he hints that expanded GPU monitoring capabilities could be coming to Windows as standard.
articles.author: Mark Tyson

articles.title: I've reviewed the Dreame L50s Pro Ultra, and it's a good robot vacuum option if you have mostly hard floors — but not so much for carpets
articles.content: When trying to find the best robot vacuum for your home, it’s important to consider all of the variables. What kind of flooring do you have in your home? Are there any pets? Children? Each robot vacuum has its strengths and weaknesses. The strengths of the Dreame L50s Pro Ultra include great cleaning on hard floors, with accurate mapping. The price point is also very attractive for the performance, and the base station is low-maintenance for busy households. However, if you have a home with carpet, this robot vac should be a skip for you as it struggles here. It also leaves some residue behind after mopping too. To find out more and see if it could be the right fit for your home, keep reading this full Dreame L50 Pro Ultra review. Dreame L50s Pro Ultra review: Specs Price £649 Robot dimensions 13.8 x 13.8 x 4.1 inches Base station dimensions 23.2 x 18.0 x 13.4 inches Suction power 30,000Pa Mapping Yes App Yes Self-emptying Yes Mop function Yes Battery 5,200mAh Runtime 171 minutes Dreame L50s Pro Ultra review: Price & availability The Dreame L50s Pro Ultra is available for £649 on Amazon U.K. in White or Black. This is a very reasonable price for the good performance you get from this robovac. This specific model isn’t available in the U.S. However, you can buy the Dreame L50 Ultra for $899 from Amazon , which has slightly lower suction power. Around a similar price is the Roomba Max 775 Complete . This robovac costs £799, and while it’s pretty loud, it will leave crisp cleaning lines behind on your carpet. (Image credit: Tom's Guide) However, I don’t love the roller mop on the Roomba. Instead, I'd recommend the Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro for £1,199. This is more expensive, but as I always say — when it comes to robovacs, you need to spend more to get good performance. Dreame L50s Pro Ultra review: Design The Dreame L50s Pro Ultra looks almost identical to the flagship Dreame X50 Ultra. Design-wise, there isn’t much that separates these two models, but their specs are very different. The base station measures 23.2 x 18.0 x 13.4 inches, but has a sleek design so it’s not an eyesore in your home. In the base station, there’s a self-emptying dustbin, along with clean and dirty water tanks. It can maintain itself for up to 100 days without taking up a lot of space. (Image credit: Tom's Guide) The robot measures 23.2 x 18.0 x 13.4 inches, which, again, is the same size as the X50 Ultra Complete. The L50s Pro Ultra looks a little different, though, since it has a sensor that is permanently deployed, unlike the retractable sensor on the X50 Ultra Complete. With the Dreame L50s Pro Ultra, you get circular mop pads that clean themselves in the docking station. I find this shape far more effective than roller mops you get with other robot vacuums such as the Roomba Max 775 Combo . (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Another sleek design feature of the L50s Pro Ultra is the extending side brush. This sweeps all of the dust and debris that can get caught up at the sides of the room into the path of the vacuum for easy cleanup. The bumper on the front of the robot is also very bouncy, and this helps prevent damage as it bumps into surroundings. Dreame L50s Pro Ultra review: App The Dreame L50s Pro Ultra uses the Dreame app. I’ve used this app before when testing other home appliances from Dreame, and its user-friendly interface is one of my favorites to use in my home. All of the controls are easily mapped out, and when you initially set up the app with your device, it gives you a walkthrough of controls. (Image credit: Tom's Guide) I like that I can adjust the operations of the vacuum each time it’s used, as I don’t need to robovac on full suction power for every single clean, so I can save some power. Dreame L50s Pro Ultra review: Mapping Mapping the ground floor of my home with the Dreame L50s Pro Ultra took around 10 minutes. This is what I’ve come to expect when initially mapping my home with a new robot vacuum. It uses a laser distance sensor…

articles.title: Enterprise AI is waiting for its Transformer moment
articles.content: As a professor of innovation, there’s a slide in my deck I use every time I start a session on artificial intelligence : a fragment of the first page from the “ Attention Is All You Need ” paper, from 2017. I use just a fragment because I don’t want the students to read it… I usually refrain from using a lot of academic papers when I teach MBAs and executives: they tend to be boring, and this one is no exception and is not particularly easy to read. However, it is historic. Written by eight Google researchers, it is the paper that defines the Transformer architecture, which among other things, became the architecture behind GPT and much of the subsequent generative- AI wave. The rest, as I said, is history. The Transformer was not only a successful model architecture: it was also a huge architectural discontinuity. The 2017 breakthrough was able to completely reorganize computation around self-attention, to eliminate recurrence and to make parallel training much easier. And in doing so, it did not simply enlarge what was already there: it completely changed the architecture . In 2017, Google understood the technology, but underestimated the category it could create. It did not ignore the Transformer: it incorporated the architecture into products such as Translate and Search, but it failed to turn its own breakthrough into the product that defined the next era. OpenAI , founded two years before the paper appeared, recognized its broader potential and built GPT, and ultimately ChatGPT , on top of it. Meanwhile, all eight authors eventually left Google, seven to become founders and one to join OpenAI. For present purposes, “Transformer moment” means an organizing principle whose eventual importance greatly exceeds its initial application. Making an artificial worker more capable versus making an organization intelligent I have been insisting on this for a long while now : an individual, human or artificial, can complete tasks, but a company, on top of that, must preserve state, coordinate specialized capabilities, enforce authority, remember outcomes and adapt across time . In that sense, transformers provided the architectural foundation for extraordinary advances in model-level and task-level capabilities. But from there, there is still a significant gap until you can reach enterprise performance. In McKinsey’s 2026 survey, 80% of respondents reported improved personal productivity, but only 37% reported a positive contribution to enterprise EBIT , with no significant differences from the previous year. This reveals the distance between individual augmentation and organizational results. McKinsey also notes that the high performers are typically those companies that redesign workflows, rather than simply inserting AI into existing ones. In practice, the industry’s current starting point seems to be the agent. Anthropic explicitly begins with the “augmented LLM” , a model supplied with retrieval, tools and memory, while Microsoft presents sequential, concurrent, group-chat, handoff and other multi-agent patterns . These are useful techniques, but nearly all begin with an artificial worker and ask how to connect it to other workers. Is coordinating agents the same thing as designing an intelligent organization? To me, at least, it looks completely different. This proliferation of patterns is the evidence of an unsettled foundation The problem is not just variety: what fails is that every implementation, each agentic project, repeatedly reconstructs the same underlying capabilities, from identity, to permissions, state, policy, evidence, recovery and learning, because no common foundation exists. If we take a look at Gartner’s forecasts, they predict that more than 40% of agentic projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027 due to cost, unclear value or inadequate risk controls. This supports the idea that model capability alone is insufficient. Gartner also explicitly recommends focusing on enterprise productivity as a whole,…

articles.title: Aaron Swartz Would've Been 40 Today.  His 'Legacy Lives On' Says FSF
articles.content: "Aaron Swartz would have turned forty this year," writes FSF deputy director Sean O'Brien. "November 8 is Aaron Swartz Day, when we remember a pioneer of free software and information sharing whose contributions helped shape the modern internet." The Internet Archive will host a hackathon Sunday in San Francisco celebrating Aaron's Swartz's life "and the projects he worked on, many of which are still going strong today," including SecureDrop, OpenLibrary, and Creative Commons. "We are also spreading the word about projects he inspired," including OnionPress and the EFF's Atlas of Surveillancedocumenting police tech use through open source research, now a collaborative effort with volunteers, the University of Nevada, Reno, and the Reynolds School of Journalism. The event is also supported by Free Law Project, and organizers are asking attendees to "bring a color print out of your favorite photos of Aaron for a huge collaborative collage." From the Internet Archive's blog: Aaron was also a co-founder of Creative Commons, where he worked with Lisa Rein developing the RSS-enhanced HTML code that sits behind Creative Commons licenses, much of which is still in use today. The "Quantifying the Commons" project was designed to help measure open-licensed and public-domain works worldwide, and is one of the projects participants can work on. Aaron loved Tor and created tools such as "Tor2web" (with Virgil Griffith) to help more people publish Tor-accessible websites. Onion Press is a Tor-based publishing system designed for decentralized, censorship-resistant publishing, and participants can work on the code base... We also encourage you to have a hackathon in your own town using our materials — or materials of your own. Please let us know if you plan to do this (although it's not required!). If you do let us know, we can include you on our website and help you spread the word about your event. So far, there is an event in Portland sponsored by Portland Civic Lab where they will be screening The Internet's Own Boy and celebrating Aaron's life. "EFF was proud to call Aaron a friend and ally," the digital rights organization posted this week. And the FSF's deputy director writes "It is particularly striking that some of the world's largest companies now rely on technology Swartz helped to develop." One of Swartz's most important technical contributions was his collaboration with John Gruber on Markdown, the simple text formatting system introduced in 2004. Markdown allows users to create structured documents using ordinary text, without requiring proprietary software. More than twenty years later, Markdown has become one of the most popular formats for documentation and publishing, and is widely used in community websites such as forums and wikis. This is not a minor contribution. Companies developing LLMs use Markdown extensively in their products and development tools. OpenAI, for example, recommends Markdown for organizing instructions and communicating structure to its ChatGPT models... Swartz also developed web.py, a public domain framework for building Python applications, and contributed to RSS 1.0, a public internet standard for distributing news and other information between websites. Swartz developed web.py while rewriting the software running Reddit after Reddit acquired Swartz's company Infogami. Reddit recently licensed its content to AI companies, and the FSF's deputy director notes "the enormous scale of the alleged 'piracy' by giant technology corporations" while Aaron himself had "faced criminal prosecution for downloading academic research that he wanted to distribute with no monetary gain." articles.title: Physicists listened to electrical noise to crack a superconductor mystery
articles.content: Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, but most only work a few degrees above absolute zero. In the late 1980s, copper-based materials called cuprates were found to superconduct at higher temperatures—reachable with affordable liquid nitrogen. Yet nearly 40 years later, physicists still don't agree on why. In a recent Science study, a team of physicists led by Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University in the Netherlands has found some answers by listening to the faint electrical crackle of current flowing into a cuprate. The missing electrons Central to the mystery of cuprates’ high-temperature superconductivity is a strange state called the pseudogap. “The pseudogap is a phenomenon of missing electrons,” Allan said. Above the temperature at which cuprates become superconducting, some of their electrons seem to vanish—measurements find far fewer of them at the energies where they should be. “Everybody knows that from different probes, you see that there's these vanishing electrons, but nobody knows why,” Allan said. articles.title: I played Android’s first AI frame-gen game: Mobile just had its DLSS moment
articles.content: Credit: Robert Triggs / Android Authority Talk of the mobile silicon town this year is, once again, AI, but this time with a twist for gamers. The latest GPU developments from Arm and Qualcomm center on similar neural upscaling techniques we’ve long seen in the PC space, using “AI” to boost frame rates and resolutions, making next-gen games look and run better without the traditional rendering costs. In a bid to showcase that this is more than just tech demo talk, Arm worked closely with developer Sumo Digital to create Neural Dawn — a light platforming title built from the ground up to use Unreal Engine’s impressive MegaLights ray-traced lighting system. The game leverages Arm’s Neural Super Sampling and Denoising (NSSD) and Neural Frame Rate Upscaling (NFRU) technologies to make this actually run on a smartphone. Version 1.0 just dropped last week, meaning we can actually go and play it.

articles.title: Doom delivers five minutes of terminal violence on an IBM mainframe
articles.content: Can an IBM Z mainframe run Doom? Of course it can. The more interesting question is whether you can play it through a text terminal without ruining your eyesight. WND Software's browser demo connects to an IBM Z mainframe over SSH using its terminal emulator. Wojciech Graj's DOOM-ASCII supplies the text-based carnage, replacing conventional graphics with colored characters. There's no sound. It is, however, completely playable (although you might need to recalibrate your vision to work out what is going on, particularly with regard to distant objects). Sessions are limited to five minutes, with room for up to 50 simultaneous users, but we had no trouble getting in. ASCII also presented no issues once the game was in motion. This writer played the original shareware release on an Amstrad ALT386SX portable, so squinting at an indistinct demon felt reassuringly familiar. That Doom can be persuaded to run on an IBM Z mainframe is not particularly noteworthy. The code has turned up everywhere from databases to PCB designers . Even the humble Pi Pico was roped into the fun. Keeping the action playable through a text terminal is the more entertaining achievement. A year ago, an IBM consultant persuaded Doom to run on IBM Z and LinuxONE using VNC to bring the pixelated mayhem to life. Using a terminal emulator, while a neat demonstration of the capabilities of WND's software, is perhaps more an example of "because I can" masochism. It's undeniably an enjoyable way to burn through five minutes. No installation or login required – just a willingness to shoot at punctuation. ®

articles.title: Google wants to lock Android down, but Droynis teaches you how to stay safe instead
articles.content: Part of the beauty of Android is its openness. It’s one of the many reasons why I would rather snag a Pixel or Galaxy device ahead of an iPhone. I can choose which default apps to employ, where I get them from, how I set up my phone, and even circumvent some restrictions if I’m feeling particularly spicy. A shortcoming of this borderless design is that Android users can often inadvertently set up an environment with potential security issues. As is so often the case with Android, that particular problem also breeds opportunity, and a new open-source app has jumped in to help Google solve it. It’s called Droynis , and it’s the security auditing tool that should’ve been a part of Android all along.

articles.title: Google AI Releases Elephant-Goldfish Model Plugin for Spec-First Coding
articles.content: Google has open-sourced the Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM) plugin , a design-and-review layer for AI coding agents. The Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin makes an agent write a specification before it writes code. Fresh subagents with no conversation history then attack that spec. Google says thousands of its engineers use it . It is quite simple: catch wrong assumptions in a Markdown file, not in a pull request. TL;DR Size: 7 skills, 9 reviewer personas, 6 brainstorm lenses, 5 review stages. No model weights; your agent supplies the LLM. Runs on: any harness that can spawn fresh subagents: Antigravity, Claude Code 2.1.271+, Claude Cowork, Codex, ChatGPT. Uses your existing model quota. Performance: no accuracy benchmark published. Evidence is adoption and end-to-end harness test runs. Best: Codex 0.163.0 completed 15 native fresh-context reviewers in order. 2 live tests passed in 573.13s. Worst: the Claude Cowork run stopped after stages 5 to 7 on a usage limit. Issue #237 reports AGENTS.md leaking into Codex reviewers. Bottom line: best thing, forced independent review before code. Worst thing, heavy token use and unverified isolation on some hosts. What is Google’s Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin? EGM is an Apache 2.0 plugin of skills, reviewer personas and document standards. It is not a new language model. The method comes from Dave Rensin’s essay on elephants and goldfish. The Google Open Source blog frames it as a fix for AI “slop” and session context collapse. The README states it is not an officially supported Google product . How does the Elephant-Goldfish workflow work? The Elephant is a long session holding project context and earlier decisions. It drafts the spec and writes no code. Each Goldfish is a stateless subagent. It reads only the draft and the files it references. You resolve trade-offs and approve the design. The core loop has 3 commands: /egm-brainstorm clarifies the idea, then runs a 6-lens Goldfish swarm. Lenses cover YAGNI, token cost, UX, migration, observability and tech debt. Output: concepts_brief.md . /egm-draft turns the brief into a design doc under docs/designs/ , section by section. /egm-review runs the Goldfish review. /egm-drift-report later compares code with the spec. The docs recommend running it weekly. What happens in the 5-stage Goldfish review? The review skill runs 5 sequential stages: Initial Zoom Out: checks the whole document at a high level. Comprehension Test: a Goldfish paraphrases the design. A wrong paraphrase means the doc is ambiguous. Critic Review: design, structural and style reviewers hunt gaps and edge cases. Intermediate Zoom Out: rechecks architecture after fixes. Implementation Readiness: checks file paths, data structures and signatures. Each stage allows at most 1 re-audit. Findings are ranked Blocker, Major or Nit. If a host has no subagent tool, EGM stops. A same-context review is not a Goldfish review. Which coding agents does EGM support? Launch coverage described Antigravity-only support , with more coming. The current harness guide covers Antigravity CLI and App, Claude Code, Claude Cowork, Codex, ChatGPT, omp and Muse. Antigravity CLI, Claude Code and Codex pass automated end-to-end fixtures. Claude Code needs version 2.1.271 or later . Reviewers there get only Read, Grep and Glob tools. CLAUDE.md files are excluded from their context. The test record gives concrete run data: Antigravity CLI 1.4.5: 16 native reviewers ran, stages in order. Codex 0.163.0: 15 native reviewers, 2 live tests in 573.13s. Codex CLI with the v0.1.0 ZIP: full suite passed in 482.30s. How does EGM compare with Spec Kit, Kiro and Superpowers? Feature Google EGM GitHub Spec Kit Kiro Specs Superpowers Type Plugin (skills + personas) Toolkit + Specify CLI Feature of an agentic IDE/CLI/web Skills plugin License Apache 2.0 MIT Commercial ( pricing ) MIT Workflow Brainstorm, draft, review, drift report Constitution, specify, plan, tasks, implement, converge…

articles.title: Which Routing Does Each MoE Model Use? DeepSeek, Qwen, Mixtral, Llama 4, gpt-oss Compared
articles.content: Open Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models share one idea but disagree on almost every routing detail. Expert counts range from 8 to 384. Top-k ranges from 1 to 8. Some models keep an always-on shared expert; others drop it. TL;DR Size: 10 models, from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (35B total, 3B active) to DeepSeek-V4-Pro (1.6T total, 49B active). Runs on: gpt-oss-120b fits one 80 GB GPU with MXFP4; DeepSeek-V4-Pro and Kimi K2 need multi-GPU expert parallelism. Performance: Routed sparsity spans 4x in Mixtral (8 experts, top-2) to 128x in Llama 4 Maverick (128, top-1). Best: Kimi K2 found sparsity 48 needed 1.69x fewer FLOPs than sparsity 8 at equal validation loss. Worst: Llama 4 Maverick and gpt-oss do not publish their gating or balancing method in config.json. Bottom line: Best thing: configs make routing fully auditable. Worst thing: names like “17B active” hide very different routers. How do open MoE models route tokens? Every model below uses token-choice routing: each token selects its own experts. They differ on 5 knobs. These are expert count, experts per token, shared experts, the scoring function and the load-balancing method. The table lists each knob per model. MoE routing comparison table (November 2026) Model Total / active params Routed experts Top-k Shared experts Gating Load balancing Mixtral 8x7B 47B / 13B 8 2 0 Softmax over top-k Aux loss, coef 0.02 ( config ) gpt-oss-120b 117B / 5.1B 128 4 0 Softmax over selected Not disclosed Qwen3-235B-A22B 235B / 22B 128 8 0 Softmax, top-k normalized Global-batch aux loss, coef 0.001 Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 35B / 3B 256 8 1 Not disclosed Aux loss, coef 0.001 (config) Llama 4 Maverick 400B / 17B 128 1 1 Not disclosed Not disclosed DeepSeek-V3 671B / 37B 256 8 1 Sigmoid Aux-loss-free bias (noaux_tc) DeepSeek-V4-Pro 1.6T / 49B 384 6 1 sqrtsoftplus noaux_tc; hash routing in 3 layers DeepSeek-V4-Flash 284B / 13B 256 6 1 sqrtsoftplus noaux_tc; hash routing in 3 layers Kimi K2 1.04T / 32B 384 8 1 Sigmoid noaux_tc + sequence aux, alpha 0.001 GLM-4.5 355B / 32B 160 8 1 Sigmoid Loss-free balance routing Sources: each model’s Hugging Face config.json, model card or technical report, verified November 7, 2026. Configs and cards for Qwen3.6 and Llama 4 omit gating. gpt-oss and Llama 4 omit the balancing method. How does DeepSeek-V3 routing work? DeepSeek-V3 scores 256 routed experts with a sigmoid, then normalizes the selected scores. A per-expert bias steers the top-8 selection without touching the mixing weights. Experts sit in 8 groups, and the router keeps 4 groups first. Each token reaches at most 4 nodes, according to the technical report . One shared expert runs for every token. What changed in DeepSeek-V4 routing? DeepSeek-V4 raises Pro to 384 routed experts but lowers top-k from 8 to 6. The score function becomes sqrtsoftplus. The first 3 MoE layers use hash routing , a fixed token-to-expert map. Bias-based noaux_tc balancing stays. How many experts does Qwen3 MoE use? Both original Qwen3 MoE models use 128 experts and route each token to 8. Qwen3 dropped the shared experts of Qwen2.5-MoE and adopted a global-batch balancing loss. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B changes course: 256 experts, 8 routed plus 1 shared, per its model card . How does Llama 4 Maverick routing differ? Llama 4 Maverick alternates dense and MoE layers. In each MoE layer, a token goes to 1 shared expert and 1 of 128 routed experts. That top-1 design echoes the Switch Transformer. It keeps 17B active parameters despite 400B in total. How does gpt-oss route tokens? gpt-oss-120b uses a linear router over 128 experts and keeps the top 4. Its config lists no shared expert. Its MoE weights ship in MXFP4, which lets the 117B model fit on a single 80 GB GPU. Why do Kimi K2 and GLM-4.5 look like DeepSeek-V3? Kimi K2 ships with the DeepseekV3ForCausalLM architecture class and the noaux_tc router. It raises routed experts to 384 at the same top-8. The Kimi K2 report found that higher sparsity lowered loss at fixed active compute.…

articles.title: The best Android browser isn’t on the Play Store. Here’s how to install it
articles.content: Credit: Andy Walker / Android Authority For anyone looking to ditch Google Chrome, the Play Store has enough options already, from privacy-focused ones like Brave to extension-friendly browsers like Firefox. But no matter which you pick, there’s something always missing, whether it’s features, customization, or just a bit of personality. Solipsism Browser is an open-source, Chromium-based browser that’s a rare exception. I don’t blame you if you haven’t heard of it — it’s fairly new and isn’t available on the Play Store either. Here’s how to install it on your Android and, more importantly, why it’s worth jumping through a few extra hoops.

articles.title: Internet governance about to get its quadrennial stress test at ITU meeting
articles.content: The International Telecommunications Union (ITU) kicks off its quadrennial plenipotentiary on Monday, and internet governance organizations are bracing in case the event becomes a forum for nation-states to try to challenge their roles. The ITU is the United Nations' specialized agency for information and communication technologies, meaning its members are nation-states. The body's role is to facilitate international connectivity, which it does by managing radio spectrum, satellite orbits, and working on relevant technical standards. Its key standards are pervasive. ITU-T X.509 sets out the rules of public key infrastructure. ITU-T E.164 governs telephone numbers. ITU-T H.264 and 265 define the video codecs used for most online streams. The ITU's role is largely uncontested, yet its work gets very close to that of the organizations who work on technologies that make the internet work. Those bodies include the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF); the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN), which oversees the domain name system; and the regional internet registries (RIRs), which manage IP addresses. The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) works on HTML, CSS, and accessibility. Governments participate in work at those internet governance bodies but are just one voice among many and can't override the consensus-driven decision-making process they use, under a system which has come to be known as the multi-stakeholder governance model. At a 2025 event called WSIS+20, the United Nations endorsed multi-stakeholder governance by deciding that its Internet Governance Forum (IGF) should become a permanent body. That decision effectively endorsed multi-stakeholder governance, and kept the ITU out of internet standards. Yet the IGF hasn't met since WSIS+20, so it is yet to start operating meaningfully as a permanent body. This year's ITU meeting is therefore a moment at which stakeholders can stress-test the delicate balance between the ITU, internet governance bodies, and the emerging IGF. Such a test could see ITU members try to have it pursue new fields that overlap with work performed by internet governance organizations. This has already happened before. China tried to have the ITU work on " New IP" – a major revision to internet protocol, a technology the IETF manages. In 2022, Russia and China backed a candidate for the ITU presidency who favored giving nations a stronger role in internet governance, potentialy by having the ITU take over some standards work. That candidate was not elected. Ahead of next week's meetings, the Internet Society published a background paper that declared it is "actively challenging proposals that could affect the Internet's underlying technical architecture or increase fragmentation, as well as those that could affect connectivity, particularly for remote, underserved, and unserved communities." The society is watching for resolutions on AI, quantum technologies, and other emerging areas that could embed specific technologies in ITU mandates. It also observes that decisions are yet to be made on which bodies should oversee governance of low-earth orbit satellite constellations, submarine cable resilience, and spectrum policy. ICANN is also watching with interest. "ICANN welcomes the recognition of the consensus-based WSIS+20 outcomes," the organization told The Register by email. "At the same time, proposals that seek to expand the ITU's role in areas such as IP-based networks, the Domain Name System, management of Internet resources, and Internet-related public policy issues raise concerns about overlapping mandates and the creation of parallel processes that could affect the health of the Internet." ICANN didn't point to any specific proposals that raise such concerns, and at ITU meetings most proposals – of which there are 278 this time around – are decided on consensus. It is, however, possible for ITU members to amend proposals during meetings, leaving open the possibility of…

articles.title: 5 books to calm AI-induced existential dread
articles.content: Artificial intelligence is transforming how we work, connect, and live. But with its extraordinary potential come some big questions about trust, human relationships, and the future of society. These five books explore the promises and perils of AI , offering fresh perspectives on a technology that’s changing our world faster than ever. Learn something new every day with “Book Bites,” 15-minute audio summaries of the latest and greatest nonfiction. Get started by downloading the Next Big Idea app today! Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines By Sherry Turkle Tracing our new habit of talking to machines through the human life cycle―from children’s earliest attachments to how we face death―Turkle offers both a cautionary tale and a road map for reclaiming our humanity in the age of AI. Listen to our Book Bite summary, read by author Sherry Turkle , or view on Amazon . Trias Algorithmica: What Code Rules By Hamilton Mann Whether you oversee digital transformation, shape regulation, or design algorithmic tools, this book provides the conceptual and practical foundations for accountable algorithmic governance. Listen to our Book Bite summary, read by author Hamilton Mann , or view on Amazon . The Eureka Machine: Why AI Is the Key to Unlocking a New Era of Scientific Discoveries By Richard Socher The most meaningful application of AI will be the automation of scientific discovery itself: a Eureka machine that combines all human knowledge, simulates billions of experiments, and generates breakthroughs. Listen to our Book Bite summary, read by author Richard Socher , or view on Amazon . Manage the Machine: How to Harness Human-AI Collaboration at Work By Paula Goldman From Salesforce’s chief ethical and humane use officer, a prescriptive guide for how to integrate AI into the workplace effectively. Listen to our Book Bite summary, read by author Paula Goldman , or view on Amazon . Human Raised: Nurturing Connection, Curiosity & Lifelong Learning in the Age of AI By Dana Suskind The challenge isn’t to reject AI as a parenting tool—it’s to use it in ways that strengthen, rather than substitute for, the messy, imperfect interactions children need to flourish. Listen to our Book Bite summary, read by author Dana Suskind , or view on Amazon . This article originally appeared in Next Big Idea Club magazine and is reprinted with permission. articles.title: I tested Bose’s new entry-level soundbar — and while it has no Dolby Atmos, its dialogue clarity beats the Sonos Beam 2 for movies and Netflix shows
articles.content: Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen review: Cheat sheet Price: 3/5 Sound quality: 4/5 Design: 5/5 Features: 4/5 Overall score: 4/5 Best for: Small spaces, small(ish) budgets Soundbars are expensive. $800, $1,500, heck, I’ve even tested $3,500 models. That’s simply inaccessible for a lot of people. And not to mention size — some of the best soundbars are almost fifty inches long. I certainly don’t have that much space in my living room. Thankfully, Bose has the answer for us small-budget, small-spaced folk. The Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen is just twenty-three inches long, making it ideal for cozy living rooms and smaller TVs. Nothing’s changed from the original — it’s still 23 inches long, 2 inches deep, and 4 inches high. So what’s different? The 2nd Gen has a center tweeter for better dialogue and high-frequency sound separation. Sometimes I read these specs and resist the urge to roll my eyes, but in the TV Speaker 2nd Gen’s case, this new tweeter really does make a difference. I never struggled to hear dialogue, on-screen sound effects are surprisingly distinct, and the extra bass button is impactful. Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen review: Specs Price $299 / £299 Connectivity HDMI, Optical Weight 4.4 pounds Dimensions 23.5 x 2.2 x 4.1 inches Colors Black Subwoofer No Dolby Atmos No Channel 3.0 Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen review: What I like There’s a lot I like about the Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen. Sound quality (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Given its small stature, I wasn’t expecting room-filling sound from the Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen. I was wrong. As soon as I set it up with my TCL TV, I had floorboard-quaking sound. I watched three movies on 4K UHD Blu-rays — “Top Gun: Maverick”, “Project Hail Mary”, and “Obsession”, and watched basic stereo TV on Now TV (the U.K.’s HBO) and Netflix. “Top Gun: Maverick” filled my testing room. I was super surprised by the expansiveness in the upper mids — the synth chords in the soundtrack came through with gusto. The rumbling of jet engines was impactful and didn’t overpower high-frequency sounds like clinking metal wheels and whirring equipment. While the whooshing ropes could have been a little louder, and I wanted a little more impact from the kick drum in the soundtrack, I was extremely happy with this performance — especially considering the soundbar’s 23 (L) x 2 (H) x 4 (D) size. Dialogue was extremely clear, even in loud action sequences. When Maverick is flying at hypersonic, the rattling cockpit and screeching air resistance didn’t overpower the in-scene mumbled dialogue. “Obsession” also sounded fantastic. The dialogue was perfectly clear, even in loud bar scenes underpinned with indistinct chatter and diegetic music. Every line filled the room. In quieter scenes, the crickets punctuated the fabric of the scene without overpowering the dialogue. (Image credit: Tom's Guide) In “Project Hail Mary”, the soundtrack’s wind instrument sections were particularly overwhelming — in an intentional way. The whirring of the spaceship was audible even over the soundtrack, and I could really feel every layer of sound. Of course, this soundbar doesn’t have Dolby Atmos, but “behind” sounds, such as doors opening, sounded as if they were coming from behind me. Stereo TV also sounded great. As not everyone has 4K Blu-rays — especially not if you need a small, cheap soundbar like this one — it’s only logical that I test it out on basic TV as well. “Supernatural” on Now TV has a great mixture of action sequences, broody dialogue, and soundtrack. Even during action sequences, I could hear every word of dialogue. Of course, the overall quality was inferior compared to 4K Blu-rays, with everything a little more muffled. I also watched “Gilmore Girls” on basic Netflix, which also has the 2.0 stereo audio track. As this is an older show, dialogue was a little softer, but this is also the case when I watch with my Denon Home 550 ($699). The TV Speaker 2nd Gen has bass boost, which does what it says on the tin. I activated this for…

articles.title: NASA Announces It's Looking for New Astronauts
articles.content: Saturday NASA officials announced it's accepting applications for a new astronaut class, reports the Associated Press: With only 32 active astronauts, the space agency needs more recruits as it looks to expand humanity's presence beyond low-Earth orbit as quickly as possible... "We have far more work than we have astronauts," Artemis III commander Randy Bresnik told The Associated Press on Saturday. Aspiring astronauts have between now and Dec. 3 to submit their applications... [They'll begin their training by early 2028]. By then "we're going to have people on the moon — so don't delay," Bresnik urged potential candidates. Bresnik and his three crewmates will blast into orbit next summer to practice docking their capsule with a pair of lunar landers, one built by Elon Musk's SpaceX and the other by Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin. Their mission will stick close to Earth — no lunar flyby — and serve as a dress rehearsal for the following year's Artemis IV mission that will attempt to land two astronauts near the lunar south pole. The moon base will materialize as more rovers, robots, structures and power grids are launched. The article notes NASA's last call for new astronauts was two years ago, and "More than 8,000 applied, with 10 making the final cut in September 2025." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: ‘The Institute’ season 2 review: Ben Barnes leads another chilling chapter in Stephen King’s twisted sci-fi thriller
articles.content: Based on Stephen King’s 2019 novel of the same name, “The Institute” is a sci-fi thriller series that first premiered on MGM+ in July 2025. Starring Ben Barnes, Mary-Louise Parker and Joe Freeman, the adaptation quickly made an impression with audiences, recording one of the best premieres in the streamer’s history. Now, the King adaptation is back, with the story continuing beyond the events of the original novel. As a fan of the first season and this genre in general, I have plenty of thoughts. Tom's Guide Verdict: 'The Institute' season 2 Rating: 3.5/5 Verdict: “The Institute” season 2 is an entertaining and ambitious return, with Joe Freeman and Ben Barnes once again delivering strong performances. While it loses some of the first season’s spark, the fresh mysteries, tense moments and room to grow make it worth watching. Where to watch: "The Institute" season 2 is streaming on MGM+ Season 2 picks up following Luke Ellis (Joe Freeman) and his friends’ escape from Dennison, as they set out to bring the Institute down for good. However, their freedom doesn’t mean they’re out of danger, with the organization already working to rebuild under the direction of a powerful new ally, tech billionaire Nolan Reeves (Alfie Allen). Meanwhile, Ms. Sigsby (Mary-Louise Parker) finds herself on the outside looking in and is determined to find a way back into the organization. With more secrets to uncover and new threats emerging, the fight against the Institute is far from over. I’ve watched the episodes ahead of their official release on MGM+ and I’m ready to share my honest thoughts on whether this Stephen King adaptation is worth your time. From its expanded storyline and returning characters to the new additions and twists, there’s plenty to get stuck into now that the first episode is streaming. ‘The Insitute’ season 2 is bigger and darker (Image credit: Chris Reardon / MGM+) Season 2 picks up almost immediately after the events of the first, with Luke and the others having escaped the Institute and desperately trying to put as much distance between themselves and the organization as possible. We initially find them fleeing on the back of a train before jumping forward four months, where the group is now hiding out in a disused construction site. Tim (Ben Barnes) is still recovering from his bullet wound, but the experience has left him tougher and more guarded, particularly when it comes to keeping the children safe. Meanwhile, Luke’s precognition abilities are kicking into full swing, making him more determined than ever to track down a specific flash drive that could bring the organization down for good. The series takes a little while to find its feet, but things start to pick up as the episodes progress. That slower approach does at least give the characters more room to breathe, with the story regularly switching between Luke and the other children and the powerful figures pulling the strings behind the Institute. (Image credit: Chris Reardon / MGM+) One of the most interesting additions is Nolan Reeves (Alfie Allen), an eccentric European tech billionaire who financially backs the organization. He’s not quite as straightforward as he first appears, and his own ambitions add another layer of mystery to the season. It’s nice to see the show introduce someone who could potentially be just as dangerous as the people already running the operation. Joe Freeman and Ben Barnes remain two of the season’s biggest strengths, delivering performances that capture very different sides of the fight against the Institute. Freeman brings plenty of determination to Luke’s search for justice, while Barnes does a good job showing how Tim’s experiences have changed him and how much he fears losing the people he’s trying to protect. Not everything works quite as well, however. The developing love triangle between Luke, Kalisha (Simone Miller) and Nicky (Fionn Laird) is one of the weaker additions, particularly because their strongest connections…

articles.title: The UK government has a plan to fix 'wild west' e-bikes, but will it work?
articles.content: If you've ever used a shared e-bike in the UK, you'll know it can be a really convenient, cheap, and environmentally friendly way to get around. They're good exercise, too. But until now, their use has been largely unregulated — and that's created some big downsides, too. Now Downing Street wants to change that. The UK government is putting forward a swathe of measures to tackle issues like e-bikes blocking the pavement, too few parking spaces, and problems with anti-social rider behaviour. “I think the fact that we are consulting on this new licensing regime means that we can start to bring some order to the chaos that some people see in some parts of big cities where these e-bike schemes, rental schemes have popped up,” Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander told the Press Association. "There are a small minority of people who choose to behave recklessly but sadly, that is true of any type of way that people move around in a town or a city, and you can’t legislate for the idiots. But we can take sensible steps to give local leaders more power over the way in which these types of schemes operate,” she added. A law has already been passed to begin the process of licensing e-bike hire companies. What's new now is this public consultation, running until the end of 2026, during which citizens, lawmakers and e-bike companies can have their say . Why is 'nuisance' e-bike parking still such a problem? Bolt is one of the e-bike companies operating in the UK (Image credit: Getty Images / Mark Kerrison) It's estimated that there are around 350,000 shared e-bike trips every day in London alone, and that's a lot of bicycles. In most regions, there are no rules about where bikes can be picked up from or left, and not enough designated parking spaces to go around — the accompanying apps simply direct users towards them via GPS. That's led to plenty of overcrowding on the pavements, and e-bikes being left in areas that make life difficult or dangerous for pedestrians. Earlier this year, e-bike hire operator Lime apologised for one of its parked e-bikes forcing a blind man into the road with his guide dog. There have also been issues with riders not being able to complete journeys because of the patchwork of different rules and guidelines across individual London boroughs. Anti-social behaviour from riders has been an issue, too : Users who hire the cycles when drunk, or in a way that endangers themselves other people around them. There have long been calls for the operators to take more responsibility for how their bikes are used. Making the operators more responsible is difficult for councils that have no real powers and very little data about how the e-bikes are being used — at the moment they're relying on the goodwill of the e-bike companies and the voluntary agreements that are in place, which is something the government wants to improve upon and formalise. What is the government proposing to do about it? (Image credit: Oli Scarff / AFP via Getty Images / Lime) There's quite a bit to dig into when it comes to the new measures. The government says there will be new parking plans that make sure e-bikes aren't "inconveniencing the public" when they're not in use, and there will be fleet management plans too, designed to reduce bike overcrowding (think limits on the total number of bikes in an area). In addition, fleets of bicycles will need to be properly maintained under the new guidelines, so you can be sure that you're getting on something safe when you ride a shared e-bike — and that pedestrians and other road users aren't going to be put in danger by a faulty battery or wheel. We recognise the current patchwork approach is confusing for riders, councils and operators, all of whom deserve greater clarity and certainty. articles.title: 7 must-visit NFL stadiums for the ultimate game day experience
articles.content: Enjoying an NFL stadium encompasses so much more than the action on the field. When you watch a game with 70,000 (give or take) other folks, there’s a communal aspect to the event, one that includes tradition, technology and, of course, plenty of food. And not every NFL stadium experience warrants equal billing. Some traditions just run deeper, events feel richer, food tastes better and memories last longer. Scouring stadiums is part of my gig. From donning a hard hat and climbing into the petals that make up the Mercedes-Benz Stadium retractable roof to exploring the bowels of Lumen Field or wandering the tailgating lots of Arrowhead Stadium to exploring every inch of SoFi Stadium, I’ve toured dozens of stadiums. Sometimes I’m with architects as they explain how sketches turned to steel, or next to chefs as they craft the latest concourse-ready concoction (salivating as I prepare to sample the creation, of course) or ensuring I don’t get grass stains as turf managers explain the intricate care required to keep the field in pristine shape. So I explored NFL stadiums for you, selecting seven spots worth the trip to gain a full picture of all that the NFL has to offer. Arrowhead Stadium – Kansas City Chiefs (Image credit: Jamie Squire/Getty) Key Stats: Opened in 1972, Arrowhead Stadium hosts 76,000 fans. Known for its ocean of parking lots around the stadium—more than 19,000 parking spaces—the Truman Sports Complex turns into a tailgating mecca. The Vibe: Clad in the red of the Chiefs, the Arrowhead Stadium fan knows their football and comes for a day of celebration that includes food, chants and raucous exuberance (a powerful 142.2-decibel crowd roar in the stadium’s history punctuates this) that just may feature two-time NFL MVP and three-time Super Bowl MVP Patrick Mahomes running the offense. Tailgating: If you’re going to tailgate in one NFL Stadium across America, this is where to do it. Set up shop in your own parking spot or enter the Chiefs’ Tailgate District for food trucks, entertainment and experiences, all four hours before the game starts. Tailgating is a way of life, with recipes passed down through generations and fans setting up in the same stall for years. John Sleezer/Kansas City Star/Tribune News Service/Getty Arrowhead Stadium Jamie Squire/Getty Technology: You don’t go to Arrowhead for the glitz and glamor of technology (part of why the Chiefs actually plan to move away from the stadium), so take in a bit more of an old-school charm, although the venue features an HDR display Arrowvision board in the east end zone, while hundreds of Sony 4K displays pepper the venue. A continuous LED ribbon board encircles the seating bowl. Arrowhead features high-density Wi-Fi, 5G DAS, walk-through security, mobile ticketing and, for the players, an underground field heating system. The Food: Obviously K.C. features barbecue . And plenty of it. Find your favorite, whether the popular Joe’s Kansas City Bar-B-Que or the Smoak BBQ for the brand-new pork belly bomb with cream, Boursin, parmesan, sour cream-and-onion chips, candied thick-cut bacon and red pepper jelly. Insider Moves: Register with the team as a designated driver and receive a free water or soda. The Must-Experience Moment: Have we mentioned the tailgating? Taking in the Chiefs Hall of Fame is a must-see attraction for fans but exploring tailgating before kickoff reigns king. The Bottom Line: Experience the Midwest hospitality in a sea of red by eating your way through the day, from well before the game to during it while experiencing a classic football experience inside the Arrowhead Stadium bowl. Lambeau Field – Green Bay Packers (Image credit: Kirby Lee/Getty) Key Stats: Opened in 1957, Lambeau Field and its 81,000 seats is the second oldest stadium in the NFL. The Vibe: No other NFL venue says community like Lambeau. Tucked into the fabric of Green Bay and its neighborhoods, the team is as much a part of the local way of life as any professional sports team…

articles.title: I recorded a short film with the Honor Magic9 Pro Max — and it legit rivals Hollywood cinema cameras
articles.content: For years, phone manufacturers have sought to legitimize their imaging chops by partnering with camera brands. Nokia with Zeiss in the aughts. Huawei with Leica in the late teens. Xiaomi with Leica. Sony and Vivo with Zeiss. OnePlus and Oppo with Hasselblad. And now there’s Honor with Arri. While some of these partnerships have merely been branding exercises, others have resulted in significant improvements in camera performance. Honor and Arri’s collaboration is definitely one of the more meaningful ones. I recently spent time with both companies in Los Angeles to learn more about what they are doing together. I was also able to go hands-on with Honor’s global Magic9 Pro Max and compare it to Arri’s Alexa Mini LF cinema camera in Arri’s studios. Finally I created a short movie using the Arri Cinema mode on Honor’s Magic9 Pro Max, which is shaping out to be one of the best camera phones around. Here’s what I learned. Magic9 Pro Max: $1287 The Honor Magic 9 Pro Max is a beast of a camera phone featuring Arri-tuned dual 200MP cameras and an 8,800mAh battery to give mobile filmmakers true Hollywood-level video recording in a pocketable form factor that gives creators an unprecedented level of control and performance that makes it rival pricey cinema camera setups. View Deal The collaboration (Image credit: Myriam Joire / Tom's Guide) If you’re not familiar with Arri , here’s what you need to know. Since 1917, this German company has earned a reputation for making intuitive-to-use, individually-calibrated cinema cameras designed to work reliably in the most demanding conditions using industry standard rigging and workflows. Arri started with compact film cameras but beginning in 2010, it became one of the leaders in digital cinema with its Alexa cameras. Besides cameras, the company offers an entire ecosystem of cinema products, including lenses and lights. Today, Alexa cinema cameras are known for the “Arri Look”, which combines industry leading dynamic-range, excellent low-light performance, accurate colors, and beautiful skin tones. If you’ve watched movies like "Sinners," "Oppenheimer," "Dune," "Blade Runner 2049," and "Gravity," you’re familiar with the Arri Look. To achieve this, Alexa cinema cameras capture footage using Arri’s LogC3 gamma curve to preserve dynamic range and color data. 3D Look-Up Tables (LUTs) are then applied during production to convert the LogC3 footage to SD or HD target color spaces, and Arri offers a Look Library with 87 unique LUTs. Custom LUTs are also an option, and this allows filmmakers to achieve the exact look they want for their movies. (Image credit: Myriam Joire / Tom's Guide) We’ve covered Honor here on Tom’s Guide before , but let me give you a quick refresher. Honor started life as one of Huawei’s sub-brands, making a range of more affordable smartphones, from budget to flagship, marketed at a younger demographic. In 2020, Huawei sold Honor to a group of investors (Shenzhen Zhixin New Information Technology Co. Ltd.), and the company’s been thriving on its own ever since. Today, Honor makes some truly impressive smartphones, including the Magic V6 , which battles Oppo’s Find N6 for best book-style folding phone on the market. The company is also a leader in silicon-carbon batteries and mobile imaging, as exemplified by the highly innovative and insanely cool Robot Phone . But while Honor’s hardware is always outstanding, its software leaves a lot to be desired. Honor and Arri’s collaboration started with the Robot Phone, which first implemented the Arri Cinema mode, Arri LogC3 capture, and Arri Looks, and is continuing with the Magic9 Pro Max, the company’s flagship. While the Robot Phone is China only, the Magic 9 Pro Max will be launched globally. Unfortunately, I can’t share much information about the global Magic9 Pro Max, but I can discuss its cameras and the Arri Cinema mode.
